rules.title: Keywords are uppercase and case-sensitive
rules.rule: Colon-prefixed SSL keywords are uppercase and case-sensitive, for example `:IF` and `:BEGINCASE`.
rules.rationale:
Keywords are matched by their exact uppercase spelling. A lowercase `:if` is
not the `:IF` keyword, so the block it was meant to open does not exist.
Identifiers and function names, by contrast, are case-insensitive.

rules.title: Keywords always carry the colon prefix
rules.rule: Bare `If`/`Else`/`EndIf`/`While`/`EndWhile` keywords: SSL keywords are colon-prefixed uppercase only (`:IF`/`:ELSE`/`:ENDIF`/`:WHILE`/`:ENDWHILE`) — a bare form is an identifier, not a keyword.
rules.rationale:
Authors coming from Visual Basic or xBase write `If`, `Else` and `EndIf`.
Without the colon these are ordinary identifiers, so the line does not parse
as the statement that was meant.

rules.title: Condition-bearing keyword lines end with a semicolon
rules.rule: Condition-bearing keyword lines are statements and end with a semicolon: `:IF condition;`, `:WHILE condition;`, `:FOR i := 1 :TO n;`. Omitting it absorbs the next line into the condition.

rules.title: :BEGINCASE needs at least one :CASE
rules.rule: `:BEGINCASE` requires at least one `:CASE` block.
rules.rationale: An empty `:BEGINCASE; :ENDCASE;` block is rejected when the script compiles.

rules.title: End each case branch with :EXITCASE
rules.rule: End each `:CASE` / `:OTHERWISE` block with `:EXITCASE;` unless multi-match behavior is intentional.
rules.rationale:
`:BEGINCASE` is not a value switch. Without `:EXITCASE`, later `:CASE`
conditions are still evaluated and more than one body can run, although
`:OTHERWISE` stays skipped once any case body has run.
rules.exceptions:
Leave `:EXITCASE` out only when several matching bodies are meant to run, and
say so in a comment.

rules.title: :EXITCASE is the last statement of its branch
rules.rule: `:EXITCASE` must be the last statement of its `:CASE`/`:OTHERWISE` branch, directly in the branch body; one nested inside `:IF`, or followed by another statement, is a compile error.
rules.rationale:
`:EXITCASE` leaves the case block from the end of a branch. It is not a
general jump, so it cannot sit inside a nested block or before more
statements in the same branch.

rules.title: Include :OTHERWISE for default handling
rules.rule: Include `:OTHERWISE` for default handling; the language does not require it.
rules.rationale:
An explicit `:OTHERWISE` shows that the unmatched case was considered, even
when it does nothing.

rules.title: One statement per line
rules.rule: Use one statement per line.
rules.rationale:
One statement per line keeps diffs, diagnostics and breakpoints aligned with
single statements.

bad.code:
:DECLARE nCount, nTotal;
nCount := 0; nTotal := 0;

rules.title: Statements and comments end with a semicolon
rules.rule: Almost every SSL statement, including comments, must end with a semicolon.
rules.rationale:
The semicolon is the statement terminator, and it is also what closes a
comment. A missing semicolon joins two statements into one that does not
parse.

rules.title: No semicolon inside comment text
rules.rule: Never include a semicolon inside comment text; the first semicolon ends the comment and the remaining text becomes executable code.
rules.rationale:
An SSL comment runs from `/*` to the first `;`, whatever kind of comment it
is: a one-line note, a file banner, a procedure doc block, or a section or
region comment. There is no separate rule for any of them. A semicolon
written as punctuation inside the text ends the comment there, and the rest
of the text is read as code.

Usually that text is not valid SSL, since two bare words in a row never form
a statement, and the script does not compile. Occasionally it reads as valid
code and runs silently: a stranded doc line such as `Parameters: none;` is a
member access on an undeclared variable, so nothing points at the broken
comment.

rules.title: Conditions are logical values
rules.rule: Conditions in `:IF`, `:WHILE` and `:CASE`, and the left operand of `.AND.`/`.OR.`, must be logical values; there is no truthy/falsy coercion, and other types, including `NIL`, raise an error.
rules.rationale:
SSL does not treat `0`, `""` or `NIL` as false. A number, string or `NIL` in
a condition raises an error when the condition runs.

`.AND.` and `.OR.` check only their left operand. When the left operand does
not decide the result, the right operand is returned unchanged:
`.T. .AND. 5` is `5` and `.F. .OR. "x"` is `"x"`. Such a result then raises
when a condition tests it, far from the expression that produced it, so keep
both operands logical.

rules.title: Prefer structured flow over :LABEL
rules.rule: Prefer structured constructs (`:IF`/`:WHILE`/`:FOR`) over legacy `:LABEL` and `Branch()` in new code.
rules.rationale:
A `Branch()` jump hides the flow of a procedure. Structured blocks show where
control goes.

rules.title: Branch() targets include the word LABEL
rules.rule: Include the word `LABEL` in a `Branch()` target: `:LABEL SKIP;` is targeted as `Branch("LABEL SKIP")`, and the match is exact, including case.
rules.rationale:
The stored label text includes the keyword, so a target without `LABEL`, or
with different spacing or case, matches no label. A literal target that
matches no label fails to compile.

good.code:
Branch("LABEL SKIP");
:LABEL SKIP;

rules.title: Branch() targets are string literals
rules.rule: Pass `Branch()` its target as a string literal. A computed target (a variable, parameter or expression) never jumps: it falls through to the next statement without an error, even when its text matches the label exactly.
rules.rationale:
A literal target is checked when the code compiles: a typo, or a target that
differs from the label in case, is a compile error instead of a silent
fall-through. A computed target never reaches a label at all: the call
falls through to the next statement, so the jump is silently lost. Where the
target depends on run-time data, choose among literal `Branch()` calls with
`:IF` or `:BEGINCASE`.

good.code:
Branch("LABEL SKIP");
:LABEL SKIP;

rules.title: Prefer positive logic
rules.rule: Prefer positive logic: when an `:IF` has an `:ELSE`, test the positive condition first.
rules.rationale:
A negated condition with an `:ELSE` makes the reader invert it twice. Swapping
the branches removes the negation.

rules.title: Do not nest IIf
rules.rule: Do not nest `IIf` calls; use `:IF` or `:BEGINCASE` for more than two outcomes.
rules.rationale:
`IIf` evaluates every argument, and nesting it hides the order of the tests.
A case block states each outcome on its own line.

rules.title: Limit block nesting to four levels
rules.rule: Limit block nesting to 4 levels.
rules.rationale:
Deeply nested blocks are hard to follow. Early returns or a helper procedure
flatten them. Four levels is the 95th percentile nesting depth of STARLIMS
12's own base layer, so deeper code is unusual even in the product itself.

rules.title: SSL arrays are 1-based
rules.rule: SSL arrays are 1-based; loop over arrays from 1 through `ALen(aArray)`.
rules.rationale:
The first element is `aItems[1]`, and index 0 is invalid. A loop from 0, or one
that stops at `ALen() - 1`, misses or overruns an element.
rules.exceptions:
Collections on .NET objects reached through colon member access are 0-based
(see `net_collections_zero_based`).

rules.title: A :FOR loop closes with :NEXT
rules.rule: `:ENDFOR`: a `:FOR` loop closes with `:NEXT`.
rules.rationale:
`:ENDFOR` is reserved but is not a usable keyword, and writing it is rejected
as a syntax error. `:NEXT` is the only closer of a `:FOR` loop.

rules.title: A space before :STEP
rules.rule: Put a space before `:STEP` in `:FOR` headers.
rules.rationale:
Without the space, `9:STEP` reads as member access on the limit expression
rather than as the `:STEP` keyword.

rules.title: Loop-control statements only inside their loop
rules.rule: Use `:EXITFOR` only inside a `:FOR` loop, `:EXITWHILE` only inside a `:WHILE` loop, and `:LOOP` only inside a `:WHILE` or `:FOR` loop.
rules.rationale:
Each statement leaves or restarts its own kind of loop. Outside that loop
there is nothing for it to act on, so it is rejected when the script
compiles.

rules.title: :FOR values are numeric
rules.rule: Keep the `:FOR` loop variable, start, limit and step numeric; a non-numeric value raises an error.
rules.rationale:
The loop compares and steps its variable arithmetically, so every value in the
header must be a number.

rules.title: Use == for exact string comparison
rules.rule: Use `==` for exact string equality; `=` is prefix-style for strings.
rules.rationale:
On strings, `=` is `.T.` when the right side is empty or the left side starts
with it, so `"Logged" = "Log"` is `.T.`. `!=` negates `==`, not `=`, so the
two are not opposites: `"Logged" != "Log"` is also `.T.`.
rules.exceptions: A deliberate prefix test may use `=`. Say so in a comment.

rules.title: Use $ for containment tests
rules.rule: Use `$` for containment tests.
rules.rationale:
`sNeedle $ sHaystack` says "contains" directly. A position search compared
with zero says the same thing less plainly.

rules.title: Bracket strings for text with many quotes
rules.rule: Use bracket strings when SQL or text contains many quotes.
rules.rationale:
SSL strings have no escape sequences. A `[text]` literal can hold both single
and double quotes without splitting the string.

good.code:
:DECLARE sNote;

sNote := [He said "it's ready"];

bad.code:
:DECLARE sNote;
sNote := "He said " + Chr(34) + "it's ready" + Chr(34);

rules.title: $ takes string operands
rules.rule: Use the `$` containment operator only on strings; non-string operands raise an error.
rules.rationale:
`$` searches one string for another. A number or array on either side raises
when the expression runs.

rules.title: Write Trim() and + instead of string minus
rules.rule: Join strings with `Trim(sFirst) + sSecond`, not `sFirst - sSecond`: on strings, `-` trims trailing spaces from the left operand and then appends, which reads like subtraction.
rules.rationale:
With two strings, `-` removes trailing space characters from the left
operand and then appends the right operand: `"Sample   " - "Analysis"` is
`"SampleAnalysis"`. Nothing is subtracted, but the expression reads like
arithmetic, and a reader who does not know this behavior misreads it.
`Trim(sFirst) + sSecond` says what happens.

The LSP reports a `-` only when both operands are known strings: string
literals, builtins that return a string, or `s`-prefixed names when
Hungarian prefixes are read as types (`--hungarian-types`). Numeric and
date subtraction are never reported.
rules.exceptions:
The two forms differ when the left value ends in whitespace other than a
space. `Trim()` removes all trailing whitespace, including tabs and line
breaks, while `-` removes only spaces, so `"Lot" + Chr(9) - "A"` keeps the
tab and `Trim("Lot" + Chr(9)) + "A"` does not. When a value can end in a
tab or line break and that character must be kept, keep the `-` and say so
in a comment.

rules.title: .NET collections are 0-based
rules.rule: Index collections on .NET objects reached via colon member access (for example `dataSet:Tables[0]`) as 0-based.
rules.rationale:
A collection exposed by a .NET object keeps .NET semantics. Writing
`dataSet:Tables[1]` out of 1-based habit silently addresses the second table.

good.code: oTable := oDataSet:Tables[0];

bad.code: oTable := oDataSet:Tables[1];

rules.title: Declare and initialize arrays before appending
rules.rule: Declare array variables before use and initialize arrays before appending.
rules.rationale:
A declared variable starts as `""`, not as an empty array, so appending to it
before assigning `{}` fails.

bad.code:
:DECLARE aItems;
AAdd(aItems, 1);

rules.title: Adjacent commas for skipped arguments
rules.rule: Use adjacent commas with no spaces for skipped optional parameters.
rules.rationale:
An empty position passes `NIL`. Adjacent commas make the skipped position
obvious; a space between them looks like a missing argument.

rules.title: Check ALen before indexing dynamic input
rules.rule: Check `ALen` before reading an index from dynamic input.
rules.rationale:
An index past the end raises. Input from a query or a caller can be shorter
than expected.

rules.title: An array index is a whole number
rules.rule: Index an array with a whole number only: a fractional index raises at run time, and division gives a whole number only when it divides evenly, so wrap a computed index in `Integer()` or otherwise guarantee a whole number.
rules.rationale:
SSL has one numeric type, and `/` always divides exactly (`3 / 2` is `1.5`),
so an index computed by division is a fraction whenever the division does not
come out even. `aItems[2.5]` and `aItems[3 / 2]` raise at run time, while
`aItems[4 / 2]` works, so code that indexes with a quotient can pass its tests
and fail on the next input size. `Integer()` makes the index a whole number on
every input.

rules.title: No NIL target for mutating array helpers
rules.rule: Do not pass `NIL` as the target array to mutating array helpers.
rules.rationale:
`AAdd`, `AFill` and the other mutating helpers change the array they are
given. With `NIL` there is no array to change, and the call fails.

rules.title: Array literals use braces
rules.rule: `[a, b]` array literals: array literals use braces `{1, 2, 3}`; square brackets are for indexing (`aRows[1]`) and are also a string literal form (`[text]`), never an array constructor.
rules.rationale: `[1, 2]` is a string literal holding the text `1, 2`, not an array.

good.code:
:DECLARE aItems;

aItems := {1, 2};

bad.code:
:DECLARE aItems;
aItems := [1, 2];

rules.title: Convert types explicitly
rules.rule: Convert types explicitly with `Val()` and `LimsString()`; only date ± number and date - date coerce.
rules.rationale:
`"Total: " + 5` raises: `+` needs two strings or two numbers. Only adding or
subtracting days on a date, and subtracting two dates, mix types.

good.code:
:DECLARE sMessage;

sMessage := "Total: " + LimsString(5);

bad.code:
:DECLARE sMessage;
sMessage := "Total: " + 5;

rules.title: Be explicit about invariant date columns
rules.rule: Be explicit about invariant/local date handling when database result materialization depends on it.
rules.rationale:
The database functions take an `aInvariantDateCols` argument that decides how
date columns come back. Leaving it to the default makes the result depend on
server settings the reader cannot see.

bad.code: aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno, logdate FROM orders");

rules.title: Look up built-in parameter types
rules.rule: Look up function parameter types before relying on coercion.
rules.rationale:
Whether a built-in rejects a wrong-typed argument depends on an installation
setting. Where it is off, a string passed for a number reads as `0` and the
call quietly returns a wrong answer, so only the documented signature tells
you what a call accepts.

bad.code: dNext := DateAdd("3/5/2026", 7);

rules.title: No spaces around member-access colons
rules.rule: Prefer no spaces around `:` in member access even though SSL accepts spaced forms.
rules.rationale:
`oEmail:Subject` reads as one operand. The formatter removes spaces around a
member-access colon.

rules.title: Member access uses a colon, not a dot
rules.rule: Use colon-chained member access (`oObj:Property`, `oObj:Method():Value`), not dot-chained access (`oObj.Property`).
rules.rationale:
The colon is SSL's member-access operator. A dot after an object is not member
access, so `oObj.Property` does not reach the property.
rules.exceptions:
Dots inside an `:INCLUDE` path and inside SQL text (`table.column`) are not
member access.

rules.title: Declare variables before use
rules.rule: Declare variables before use with `:DECLARE`.
rules.rationale:
An undeclared name is looked up in the callers' scopes and then among the
public variables. A write to it can change a caller's variable, and a typo in
a read goes unnoticed.
rules.exceptions:
Predefined installation globals such as `CRLF` are read without a
declaration; declaring one hides it.

bad.code:
:DECLARE nTotal;
nTotal := nCount + 1;

rules.title: :DECLARE takes no initializer
rules.rule: `:DECLARE` initializers (`:DECLARE x := 1;`): `:DECLARE` takes bare identifiers only — assign in a separate statement. Class constants are assigned in the Constructor.
rules.rationale: `:DECLARE` only creates names. A value goes in an assignment on the next line.

good.code:
:DECLARE nCount;

nCount := 1;

bad.code: :DECLARE nCount := 1;

rules.title: Re-declaring a variable keeps its value
rules.rule: Re-declaring an existing variable with `:DECLARE` is silently ignored — no error, existing value preserved.
rules.rationale:
A second `:DECLARE` does not reset the variable. Code that relies on it to
start fresh keeps the old value.

rules.title: Variable lookup order
rules.rule: Variable lookup: local scope → caller scopes (up call stack) → public variables (`:PUBLIC`).
rules.rationale:
A name that is not local is found in a caller's scope before the publics, so a
procedure can read or change its caller's variable by accident.

rules.title: Prefer :DECLARE over :PUBLIC
rules.rule: Prefer `:DECLARE` with parameter passing over `:PUBLIC` variables, which any procedure on the call stack can read or overwrite.
rules.rationale:
A public variable outlives the procedure that declared it and is shared with
everything that runs after it, so any of that code can change it.

bad.code:
:PUBLIC nTotal;
nTotal := 0;

rules.title: Parameters are accessed by name
rules.rule: Positional parameter access (`$1`, `$2`, ...): parameters are accessed only by the names declared in `:PARAMETERS`.
rules.rationale:
SSL has no argument list to index. Each parameter is a named variable from the
`:PARAMETERS` line.

rules.title: A bare call is a built-in function call
rules.rule: A bare `Name(...)` call always means a built-in function, in scripts and classes alike; any other name stops the script from compiling with `Invalid built-in function: Name`.
rules.rationale:
The name in a bare call is looked up among the built-in functions only. A
procedure in the same script is not found that way.

good.code:
:DECLARE sName;

sName := AllTrim(" admin ");

bad.code:
:DECLARE n;
n := MyProc(1);

rules.title: Keep parameter lists short
rules.rule: Keep procedures to at most 8 parameters; more than 20 parameters on a procedure or method draws a warning, so group related state into arrays or objects.
rules.rationale:
A long positional parameter list is easy to call in the wrong order. Past 20
parameters the platform itself warns.

bad.code:
:PROCEDURE SaveOrder;
	:PARAMETERS sOrdNo, sCust, sSite, dLogged, nQty, nPrice, sUnit, sNote, bRush;

rules.title: A long procedure is a prompt to check its responsibilities
rules.rule: Treat a procedure or class method with more than 80 code lines (blank and comment lines excluded) as a prompt to check whether it has more than one responsibility, and extract procedures if it does; the number is a review trigger, not a limit.
rules.rationale:
Most procedures are short. In STARLIMS 12's own base layer three procedures in
four have at most 32 code lines, and the 95th percentile is about 83, so a
procedure past 80 code lines is among the longest one in twenty of the
product's own procedures. Class methods run shorter still (95th percentile 61). Length alone is not a
defect, but a long procedure often does several things, such as validating
input, reading data, applying a policy and writing a result, and each of those
is easier to read, test and change as its own procedure (refactoring guide,
§6.1 Extract Procedure).
rules.exceptions:
A procedure that does one thing at length, such as a single long SQL statement
or a linear sequence of steps that only make sense together, stays as it is.
Never split a procedure only to get under the number, and never collapse
distinct responsibilities or remove demonstrated guards to shorten it.

rules.title: Parameter defaults by type
rules.rule: Default a parameter to the empty value of its prefix type: `""` for strings, `0` for numbers, `.F.` for booleans, `{}` for arrays, and `NIL` for dates, objects, code blocks and variants.
rules.rationale:
A default of the parameter's own type keeps the prefix true for the value the
procedure actually receives, so code that tests or uses the value does not
meet an unexpected type.

rules.title: An SSL comment has no */ closer
rules.rule: `*/` comment closers: an SSL comment opens with `/*` and ends at the first `;`. End every comment with `;` alone — the form `; */` leaves an inert `*/` outside the comment and draws a diagnostic.
rules.rationale:
A C-style `*/` is ordinary comment text in SSL. A comment written as
`/* text */` with no semicolon runs on through the following lines until the
next `;`, so the code it swallows never runs.

rules.title: Spaces around binary operators
rules.rule: Use spaces around assignment, arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators.
rules.rationale:
Spaced operators separate the operands at a glance, and the formatter
produces this layout.

good.code:
:DECLARE nTotal;

nTotal := 1 + 2;

bad.code:
:DECLARE nTotal;
nTotal:=1+2;

rules.title: Comment regions for editor grouping
rules.rule: Use `/* region` / `/* endregion` comments for editor grouping instead of `:REGION` / `:ENDREGION`.
rules.rationale:
`:REGION` is a working construct: it stores its body as text for
`GetRegion()`. Code placed inside it is not run as code. Comment regions only
fold in the editor.

rules.title: Tabs for indentation
rules.rule: Prefer tabs for indentation; if the file already uses spaces, preserve 4-space indentation.
rules.rationale:
Tabs are the house style and what the formatter emits. Converting an existing
space-indented file wholesale buries the real change in an unreadable diff.

rules.title: Major sections open with a short summary
rules.rule: Begin major sections (procedures, classes, regions) with a short summary.
rules.rationale:
A one-line summary at the top of a procedure, class or region lets a reader
decide whether to read the section without reading all of it.

rules.title: Comments are sentence-case and concise
rules.rule: Use sentence-case and keep comments concise.
rules.rationale:
Short, sentence-case comments read as prose and do not compete with the code
for attention.

rules.title: Single-line comment form
rules.rule: Write a single-line comment as `/* comment text here;`.
rules.rationale:
The comment opens with `/*` and its own semicolon closes it. Without that
semicolon the comment never ends.

rules.title: Multi-line comment layout
rules.rule: Lay out a multi-line comment with `/*` alone on the first line, then the text lines, then `;` alone on the last line.
rules.rationale:
The language accepts any layout, because the comment ends at the first
semicolon. Putting the delimiters on their own lines makes the start and end
of a long comment easy to find.
rules.exceptions:
The file banner and procedure header templates carry the delimiters on their
star rules.

rules.title: Indent block bodies one level
rules.rule: Indent the body of a block one level: `:IF`, `:WHILE`, `:FOR`, `:BEGINCASE`, `:TRY`, `:PROCEDURE`, `:REGION` and `:BEGININLINECODE` open an indented body, and each nested block adds one more level.
rules.rationale:
Indentation shows which statements a block controls. One level per block, in
tabs or in the file's existing 4 spaces, is the layout the formatter produces.

rules.title: Closing keywords dedent to their block
rules.rule: Dedent a closing keyword to the level of the keyword that opened its block: `:ENDIF`, `:ENDWHILE`, `:NEXT`, `:ENDCASE`, `:ENDTRY`, `:ENDPROC`, `:ENDREGION` and `:ENDINLINECODE`.
rules.rationale:
A closing keyword at the level of its opening keyword marks where the block
ends, so a reader can match the pair by eye.

rules.title: Branch keywords sit at the block level
rules.rule: Put `:ELSE`, `:CASE`, `:OTHERWISE`, `:CATCH` and `:FINALLY` at the level of the keyword that opened their block, then indent the body that follows them one level.
rules.rationale:
These keywords end one branch of a block and start the next, so they line up
with the keyword that opened the block and their bodies are indented like any
other block body.

rules.title: :EXITCASE indents like a statement
rules.rule: Indent `:EXITCASE` at the level of the other statements in its branch; it does not change the indentation.
rules.rationale:
`:EXITCASE` is a regular statement of the branch, like a `break`, not a
closing keyword, so it does not dedent.

rules.title: Consistent indentation in a file
rules.rule: Keep indentation consistent within a file; do not mix tabs and spaces.
rules.rationale:
Tabs and spaces render at different widths in different editors, so a file
that mixes them shows a block structure that is not the real one.

rules.title: A space after each comma
rules.rule: Put a space after each comma and none before it.
rules.rationale:
A space after each comma separates arguments and list items at a glance, and
it is what the formatter produces.
rules.exceptions:
Skipped optional arguments keep their commas adjacent, with no space between
them (`RunSQL(sSql,, aValues)`).

good.code:
:DECLARE aItems;

aItems := {1, 2, 3};

bad.code:
:DECLARE aItems;
aItems := {1 ,2,3};

rules.title: No spaces inside parentheses
rules.rule: Do not put spaces just inside parentheses: `DoProc("Name", {args})`, not `DoProc( "Name", {args} )`.
rules.rationale:
Parentheses already delimit the argument list; spaces inside them only widen
the line.

good.code:
:DECLARE nLength;

nLength := Len("abc");

bad.code:
:DECLARE nLength;
nLength := Len( "abc" );

rules.title: No space before a call parenthesis
rules.rule: Do not put a space between a function name and its `(`: `Len(sValue)`, not `Len (sValue)`.
rules.rationale:
Keeping the parenthesis against the name marks the line as a call and matches
how the reference documents every function.

good.code:
:DECLARE nLength;

nLength := Len("abc");

bad.code:
:DECLARE nLength;
nLength := Len ("abc");

rules.title: SSL lines of about 90 characters
rules.rule: Keep SSL lines to about 90 characters, breaking longer ones at logical points.
rules.rationale:
Lines that fit in one view can be read and compared without horizontal
scrolling. SQL inside strings has its own limit in `sql_max_line_length`.

rules.title: Where to break a long statement
rules.rule: Break a multi-line function call after a comma and a multi-line condition before `.AND.` or `.OR.`, and indent each continuation line one level.
rules.rationale:
A line that ends after a comma, or starts with `.AND.`, tells the reader the
statement continues, and one level of continuation indent keeps it apart from
the next statement.

rules.title: Continuation lines take no semicolon
rules.rule: Do not end a continuation line of a multi-line statement with a semicolon; only the line that completes the statement takes one.
rules.rationale:
A semicolon ends the statement wherever it appears, so a semicolon at the end
of a continuation line cuts the statement in two and leaves the rest as an
invalid statement of its own.

rules.title: One blank line between procedures
rules.rule: Put one blank line between procedures.
rules.rationale: One blank line separates procedures without spreading a file out.

rules.title: One blank line between sections and regions
rules.rule: Put one blank line between logical sections and between regions: after the declarations, before a control block that follows code and after its closer when more code follows, before a section comment that follows code, and before a procedure's final `:RETURN`; add none at the start or end of a body.
rules.rationale:
A blank line marks where one step of the logic ends and the next begins.
Naming the boundaries makes the layout the same in every file: the
declarations stand apart from the work, each control block reads as one
unit, a section comment opens the code it describes, and the result a
procedure returns is easy to find.
rules.exceptions:
Consecutive declarations stay together, a comment between two declarations
stays with them, and a comment directly above a block or the final
`:RETURN` takes the blank line above itself instead of being separated from
the code it describes. Blank lines an author added elsewhere are kept.

rules.title: No runs of blank lines
rules.rule: Do not leave three or more consecutive blank lines; reduce such a run to two.
rules.rationale:
A run of blank lines suggests a missing piece of code and pushes the rest of
the logic off the screen. One or two blank lines are an author's grouping and
stay.

rules.title: endregion takes no name
rules.rule: Close a comment region with `/* endregion;` alone; `endregion` takes no name, so never append one.
rules.rationale:
Regions pair last-opened-first-closed, so a name on the closer matches nothing
and only suggests a pairing that does not exist.

rules.title: Align related elements
rules.rule: Align related elements, such as parameters and SQL statements, for readability.
rules.rationale:
Elements that line up can be compared at a glance, such as the parameter names
of a doc block or the clauses of a SQL statement.

rules.title: The absent-value literal is NIL
rules.rule: `NULL`: the absent-value literal is `NIL` (and the boolean literals are `.T.` and `.F.`).
rules.rationale:
`NULL`, `null`, `true` and `false` are not literals in SSL; they read as
variable names. The literals are `NIL`, `.T.` and `.F.`.

bad.code:
vValue := NULL;
bDone := false;

rules.title: Built-in values have only native .NET members
rules.rule: Strings, numbers, booleans, dates and arrays have no SSL-defined members; a `:` call reaches a case-sensitive native .NET member or raises (arrays have `:Length`, not `:Count`).
rules.rationale:
A `:` call on a built-in value goes straight to the underlying .NET object.
Its member names are case-sensitive, and a name the .NET type does not have
raises when the call runs.

rules.title: Code blocks are not compared
rules.rule: Do not compare code blocks with `=` or `==`; the comparison raises an error.
rules.rationale:
A code block has no value to compare. Comparing two of them raises when the
expression runs.

rules.title: Code block literal shape
rules.rule: Write a code block as `{|params| expression}`, with at least one parameter and a single-expression body.
rules.rationale:
A code block is one expression with its bound variables. It has no statement
list, and it needs at least one bound variable: a code block with none, such
as `{|| 1}`, does not compile.

good.code:
:DECLARE fnDouble;

fnDouble := {|x| x * 2};

bad.code:
:DECLARE fnOne;
fnOne := {|| 1};

rules.title: Check for NIL before arithmetic or string operations
rules.rule: Check for `NIL` before using a value in arithmetic or string operations; test `v == NIL` when `0`, `.F.` or an empty string is a valid value, because `Empty()` is also `.T.` for those.
rules.rationale:
`NIL + 1` and `NIL + "x"` raise. `Empty()` is `.T.` for `NIL` but also for `0`,
`.F.` and `""`, so it is not a `NIL` test when those are valid values.

bad.code:
:DECLARE nCount;
nCount := NIL + 1;

rules.title: NIL is not an empty string, zero or .F.
rules.rule: Do not treat `NIL` as an empty string, zero or `.F.`; declared variables start as an empty string, not `NIL`.
rules.rationale:
`NIL = ""` is `.F.`. A freshly declared variable holds `""`, so a `NIL` test
on it is never true.

good.code:
:DECLARE sName, bMissing;

bMissing := sName == "";

bad.code:
:DECLARE bMissing;
bMissing := NIL == "";

rules.title: One numeric type
rules.rule: SSL has one numeric type for whole and fractional values. The underlying native type varies with the value (whole numbers report `System.Int32`, fractions `System.Double`).
rules.rationale:
There is no integer type, so division always gives a fractional result
(`5 / 2` is `2.5`). The native `:` members differ between whole and fractional
values.

good.code:
:DECLARE nHalf;

nHalf := Integer(5 / 2);

bad.code: nHalf := 5 / 2;

rules.title: Assignment is :=
rules.rule: `=` assignment: assignment is `:=` (plus `+=`, `-=`, ...); `x = y` is a comparison expression, never an assignment.
rules.rationale:
`=` is the loose equality operator. Written as a statement, `nCount = 1;`
compares and throws the result away, so the variable never changes.

good.code:
:DECLARE nCount;

nCount := 1;

bad.code:
:DECLARE nCount;
nCount = 1;

rules.title: Prefer != for not-equals
rules.rule: Prefer `!=` over `<>` or `#` for not-equals.
rules.rationale:
The three operators behave the same. Using one of them everywhere keeps
comparisons easy to scan.

rules.title: One assignment per statement
rules.rule: Prefer one assignment per line; use a chained assignment only when every target should receive the same value, and do not use an assignment inside a larger expression.
rules.rationale:
Assignment is right-associative and evaluates to the assigned value, so
`sStatus := sDefault := "PENDING";` is valid. A pure chain like that, where
every target receives the same value, is the one accepted form.

The reported case is an assignment used inside a larger expression, such as
`nTotal := (nCount := 5) * 2;` or an assignment passed as a call argument.
The second assignment hides inside the first, and a reader scanning for
where `nCount` changes does not see it. Write it as its own statement.

An assignment that is the whole `:IF`, `:WHILE` or `:CASE` condition is
usually a typo for `=` or `==`. Tools report that case separately, as a
warning (`assignment_in_condition`), and not under this rule. An assignment
inside a larger condition, such as `:WHILE (nIndex += 1) <= nLast;`, is
this rule's case.

good.code:
:DECLARE sStatus, sDefault;

sStatus := sDefault := "PENDING";

bad.code:
:DECLARE nCount, nTotal;
nTotal := (nCount := 5) * 2;

rules.title: Use ++ and -- as statements of their own
rules.rule: Use `++` and `--` as a statement of their own (`nCount++;`), not inside a larger expression; never apply them to the same variable twice in one expression, or to a variable the same expression also reads.
rules.rationale:
`++` and `--` change the variable and also produce a value: postfix
(`nIndex++`) produces the value before the change and prefix (`++nIndex`)
the value after it. Inside a larger expression the reader has to work out
which value is used, and readers often get it wrong. Operands are evaluated
left to right and each `++` takes effect before the next operand is read,
so with `i = 1`, `i++ + i++` returns `3` (`1 + 2`) and leaves `i` at `3`.
As a statement of its own, `nCount++;` has one meaning: add one.

The rule has two tiers. An increment or decrement inside a larger
expression (`nNext := nCount++;`) is an info finding. Using the same
variable's `++` or `--` more than once in one expression, or incrementing a
variable that the same expression also reads (`aSeen[nIndex++] := nIndex;`),
is the case readers misjudge, and the LSP reports it as a warning
(`increment_as_statement` at warning severity instead of info).

rules.title: Use IIf, not a ternary operator
rules.rule: The C ternary `cond ? a : b`: use `IIf(bCondition, vTrue, vFalse)` (exactly three arguments; both branches are evaluated).
rules.rationale:
SSL has no `?:` operator. `IIf` is an ordinary function, so both value
arguments are evaluated before it chooses one.

bad.code: sLabel := nCount > 0 ? "some" : "none";

rules.title: Logical operators keep their periods
rules.rule: Write the logical operators with their periods: `.AND.`, `.OR.` and `.NOT.`, never bare `AND`, `OR` or `NOT`.
rules.rationale:
SSL has no bare `AND`, `OR` or `NOT` operator. A bare word between two
operands is read as an identifier, so the condition does not mean what it
says.

rules.title: Parenthesize a negated comparison
rules.rule: Write a negated comparison as `.NOT. (a = b)`: `.NOT.` binds before the comparison operators, so `.NOT. a = b` negates `a` alone.
rules.rationale:
`.NOT.` applies to the operand right after it, before any comparison is
evaluated. `.NOT. sCode = "AB"` therefore means `(.NOT. sCode) = "AB"`: on a
string, `.NOT.` raises at run time ("the operator/method: .NOT. is not
implemented on type: SSLString"), and on a logical it silently computes
`(.NOT. b) = x` instead of the negated comparison. Parentheses make the
expression mean what it says.

`!=` and `#` compare exactly, like `==`, so `sCode != "AB"` is the same as
`.NOT. (sCode == "AB")`. Neither is a drop-in replacement for
`.NOT. (sCode = "AB")`, which negates `=`'s prefix match.

rules.title: Parenthesize an expression that mixes .AND. and .OR.
rules.rule: Parenthesize an expression that mixes `.AND.` and `.OR.`: `.AND.` binds tighter, so `bA .OR. bB .AND. bC` means `bA .OR. (bB .AND. bC)`.
rules.rationale:
`.AND.` binds tighter than `.OR.`, so `bA .OR. bB .AND. bC` is evaluated as
`bA .OR. (bB .AND. bC)`, whatever the line breaks suggest. Both operators
also skip their right operand once the result is known: in
`.T. .OR. X .AND. Y`, the whole `X .AND. Y` is the right operand of
`.OR.`, so neither `X` nor `Y` is evaluated. A reader who groups the
expression left to right expects `Y` to run and to decide the result.

Adding parentheses never changes what a correct expression does, and it
states which grouping was meant. Without them, a reader cannot tell a
deliberate grouping from a mistake.

rules.title: A large server script is a prompt to check its responsibilities
rules.rule: Aim for server scripts of up to about 200 code lines with at most one local procedure; treat a server script with more than 400 code lines or more than 12 local procedures as a prompt to check its responsibilities: organize it into responsibility-based regions first, and move a responsibility to a separate script only when it is reusable on its own or independently owned.
rules.rationale:
Most server scripts are small. In STARLIMS 12's own base layer the median
script has 21 code lines, the 95th percentile about 200, and most scripts have
no local procedures at all; the few large scripts are nearly always broken
into procedures. That shape, up to about 200 code lines with zero or one local
procedure, is the one to aim for. Code written on top of the product tends to
run larger, so the review trigger is deliberately generous: a script past 400
code lines or 12 local procedures is well beyond the product's own top of
normal and likely holds more than one responsibility. Regions that group related
procedures by responsibility make such a script navigable without changing how
it runs. Moving a responsibility to its own script has a cost: a call through
`ExecFunction` resolves its string target at run time and crosses into a
separate deployment unit, where a local `DoProc` stays inside the file. Pay
that cost only for a responsibility that is reusable on its own or owned
independently.
rules.exceptions:
The 200-line, one-procedure shape is a target, and the 400-line,
12-procedure numbers are review triggers; neither is a limit. Never split a script only to get
under them, and never collapse distinct responsibilities or remove
demonstrated guards to shorten it.

bad.code:
/* 520 code lines and 15 local procedures in call order, with validation,
   persistence and notification procedures interleaved and no regions;

rules.title: Return early on invalid requests
rules.rule: Return early for invalid requests and failed contracts.
rules.rationale:
An early return keeps the success path at one indentation level and makes each
rejection visible where it happens.

rules.title: :BEGINCASE for a choice among several
rules.rule: Use `:BEGINCASE` when choosing among several routes, result shapes, artifact kinds, actions or outcomes.
rules.rationale:
A `:BEGINCASE` lists the choices side by side at one level, where a chain of
`:IF`/`:ELSE` nests a little deeper for each one.

rules.title: No :EXITCASE after a branch :RETURN
rules.rule: Do not add `:EXITCASE;` after a branch-level `:RETURN`; the return already terminates the procedure.
rules.rationale: The `:EXITCASE` can never run, and it suggests that the branch might continue.

rules.title: No duplicate outcome branches
rules.rule: Do not duplicate identical outcome branches; keep separate branches only when their behavior differs.
rules.rationale:
Two branches with the same body make a reader look for a difference that is
not there, and the copies drift apart over time.

rules.title: A linear success path
rules.rule: Prefer a linear success path over nested `:IF` chains.
rules.rationale:
When each check returns on failure, the success path reads top to bottom at
one level, instead of at the bottom of a nest.

rules.title: No control-flow exits inside :FINALLY
rules.rule: Do not use `:RETURN`, `:EXITFOR`, `:EXITWHILE`, or `:LOOP` inside `:FINALLY`.
rules.rationale:
`:FINALLY` always runs to its end, whether the protected statements finished
or raised. Each of these statements would leave it early, so each is a
compile-time error inside `:FINALLY`.

rules.title: Protect transactional work with :TRY
rules.rule: Use `:TRY`/`:CATCH` around multi-step transactional database work.
rules.rationale:
A failed write raises under the default SQL error settings. Without a `:TRY`
around the writes, nothing ends the transaction on that path, and the
operation cannot report the failure in its own result shape.

rules.title: Read error details with GetLastSSLError
rules.rule: Use `GetLastSSLError()` inside `:CATCH` to retrieve error details.
rules.rationale:
`:CATCH` does not bind the error to a name. `GetLastSSLError()` returns the
`SSLError` object, with `:Description`, `:Code`, `:Operation` and the full
diagnostic text.

bad.code: :CATCH oErr;

rules.title: Make rollback explicit for partial-failure writes
rules.rule: Make rollback behavior explicit for write operations that can partially fail.
rules.rationale:
When the second of two writes fails, either both are undone or the first one
stays. The code should show which: a commit flag that is `.T.` only after
every write passed, and an `EndLimsTransaction` call that uses it.

good.code:
bCommit := .F. before the writes
bCommit := .T. as the last statement of the :TRY body
:FINALLY ends the transaction with EndLimsTransaction(, bCommit)

bad.code:
:FINALLY ends the transaction with EndLimsTransaction(, .T.)
whatever happened in the :TRY body

rules.title: Transaction boundaries are explicit in specs and refactors
rules.rule: Do not leave transaction boundaries implicit in specs or refactors.
rules.rationale:
Which procedure begins and ends a transaction decides what a failure rolls
back. A spec or refactor that does not say so leaves the implementer to
guess, and moving a write across that boundary changes behavior silently.

good.code:
Spec: WriteStatus owns the transaction for the status UPDATE and the audit
INSERT. ChangeStatus does not begin one; it calls WriteStatus and returns its
envelope.

bad.code: Spec: ChangeStatus updates the status and writes the audit row.

rules.title: The service that owns the writes owns the transaction
rules.rule: The service that owns a related set of writes owns the transaction; coordinators delegate mutations rather than wrap an entire workflow in one broad transaction.
rules.rationale:
A broad transaction holds locks across steps that do not need to be atomic,
and makes every failure roll back unrelated work. The procedure that performs
a set of related writes knows what must commit together.

good.code: Main -> ValidateRequest -> WriteStatus (begins and ends its own transaction)

bad.code:
Main begins a transaction, then calls ValidateRequest, LoadSettings,
WriteStatus and NotifyOwner, and ends it at the end of the workflow.

rules.title: Atomic writes share one transaction
rules.rule: Keep writes that form one atomic command in the same transaction.
rules.rationale:
Writes that must succeed or fail together, such as a status change and its
audit row, can only be undone together when they commit together.

good.code:
BeginLimsTransaction
  UPDATE sample status
  INSERT sample_audit row
EndLimsTransaction(, bCommit)

bad.code:
BeginLimsTransaction, UPDATE sample status, EndLimsTransaction
BeginLimsTransaction, INSERT sample_audit row, EndLimsTransaction

rules.title: End only the transaction you began
rules.rule: Match each successful `BeginLimsTransaction` with exactly one `EndLimsTransaction` for the same connection, and end only a transaction the command started.
rules.rationale:
Each successful `BeginLimsTransaction` adds a level of depth. An extra
`EndLimsTransaction` closes the caller's transaction, and a missing one
leaves a level open after the command returns.

rules.title: The commit flag starts .F.
rules.rule: Start the commit flag at `.F.` and set it `.T.` only after the last write and verification succeed.
rules.rationale:
A raised error skips the rest of the `:TRY` body, so a flag keeps whatever
value it had. A flag that starts `.T.` and is cleared only by the checks the
code makes commits the writes that ran before an unexpected error.

rules.title: End the transaction from :FINALLY when it started
rules.rule: From `:FINALLY`, call `EndLimsTransaction(, bCommit)` only when the transaction started.
rules.rationale:
`:FINALLY` runs on success and on error, so it is the one place that always
closes the transaction. Guarding the call with the started flag means an
error raised before `BeginLimsTransaction` does not end a transaction this
command never began.

rules.title: Guard transaction finalization in envelope commands
rules.rule: In a command that returns its own failure envelope, protect the `EndLimsTransaction` call in `:FINALLY` with a nested `:TRY`/`:CATCH`, because finalization failures raise rather than returning `.F.`; on a finalization failure, fail the operation with a distinct stable code.
rules.rationale:
A commit can fail after every write succeeded. That raises from inside
`:FINALLY`, escaping the command's own `:CATCH`, so a command that promises a
result envelope has to catch it there and report the operation as failed.
rules.exceptions:
A raise-only helper that lets every failure propagate does not need the
nested guard; the finalization error reaches its caller's `:CATCH` like any
other.

rules.title: IsInTransaction decides ownership
rules.rule: Use `IsInTransaction` to establish transaction ownership or to require an existing transaction when that is part of the procedure contract; do not reject an ambient transaction merely because nesting is possible.
rules.rationale:
A command that runs inside a caller's transaction takes part in it; refusing
to run there breaks callers that compose commands.

rules.title: Replay-aware mutations
rules.rule: In a replay-aware mutation, lock the candidate row, distinguish fresh work from an exact replay, validate a versioned receipt fingerprint, reject changed requests as conflicts, and preserve the canonical receipt serialization byte for byte.
rules.rationale:
A replayed request must return the original outcome without doing the work
twice, and a changed request with the same key must not be mistaken for a
replay.

good.code:
1. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the row for the request key.
2. No row: do the work and store the receipt with its fingerprint version.
3. A row whose fingerprint matches: return the stored receipt unchanged.
4. A row whose fingerprint differs: return a conflict.

bad.code:
1. Read the row for the request key without a lock.
2. A row exists: do the work again and overwrite the receipt.

rules.title: Parse simple delimited input in SSL
rules.rule: Parse simple delimited input locally with helpers such as `BuildArray` when the rules depend only on element count, emptiness, length or exact text; normalize entries before validating and keeping the canonical list, and treat empty input or a normalization failure as no preference when the list is only an optional selection hint. Do not add a database dependency solely to split or validate text.
rules.rationale:
Splitting and checking text needs nothing from the database. A query used only
for that adds a dependency, a round trip and a failure mode.

rules.title: AllTrim to normalize input text
rules.rule: Use `AllTrim` when normalizing caller input, route values, settings text or external response text; `Trim` strips trailing whitespace only.
rules.rationale:
Text from outside the script can carry leading as well as trailing whitespace,
and `Trim` leaves the leading part in place.

rules.title: Compose text with sFmt:Format
rules.rule: Declare `sFmt` with the other string locals and use `sFmt:Format(template, {value1, value2, ...})` for messages, paths, setting keys and other composed text.
rules.rationale:
A template shows the finished text in one piece, where a chain of
concatenations hides it between the quotes.

rules.title: Format takes one array of values
rules.rule: Pass `sFmt:Format` one array holding every replacement value, including for a single placeholder.
rules.rationale:
The replacement values travel as one array; a scalar in that position is not
spread into the placeholders.

rules.title: AScanExact for fixed sets of values
rules.rule: Use `AScanExact({...}, value)` when testing membership in a fixed set of exact values; `AScan` matches strings by prefix.
rules.rationale:
`AScan` matches strings by prefix: `"APP"` matches `"APPROVED"`, and an empty
string matches the first string element.

rules.title: No bare DoProc targets in class methods
rules.rule: Do not call `DoProc` with a bare procedure name inside class methods; it is a compile-time error. Use `Me:Method()` or `Base:Method()`.
rules.rationale:
Inside a class method, a string-literal `DoProc` target with a single segment
is rejected when the class compiles. Methods on the class or its base are
reached through `Me:` and `Base:`.
rules.exceptions:
A fully qualified `DoProc("Category.Script.Procedure", {args})` that calls a
deployed script procedure compiles and runs inside a class method, and so does
`ExecFunction("Category.Script.Procedure", {args})`. A target held in a
variable is not checked when the class compiles.

rules.title: ExecFunction never targets a class file
rules.rule: Point `ExecFunction` at a script entry point or script procedure, never at a class file; create class instances with `CreateUdObject` and call their methods.
rules.rationale:
A class file defines a class, not a script. It has no top-level code to run,
so `ExecFunction` on it fails when it runs. Instantiate the class with
`CreateUdObject("Category.ClassName")` and call the method on the instance.

bad.code: ExecFunction("Samples.Counter.Increment");

rules.title: Access modifiers do nothing on class methods
rules.rule: Do not put `/*@private;` or `/*@protected;` on class methods; they affect script procedures only, and class methods are always public.
rules.rationale:
On a class method the annotation changes nothing, so it tells a reader the
method is private when any caller can reach it.

rules.title: One state object for a multi-step operation
rules.rule: For a multi-step operation, create one descriptive UDObject, initialize every property during request construction, and pass that object through cohesive steps rather than growing long positional parameter lists.
rules.rationale:
Every step sees the same named state, and a new piece of state is a new
property, not a new parameter on every procedure.

bad.code: DoProc("ApplyStep", {sOrdNo, bValid, nCount, sCode, sMessage, bStarted, bCommit});

rules.title: :PARAMETERS comes before any other statement
rules.rule: `:PARAMETERS` must appear before any other statements in a script or procedure body.
rules.rationale:
A script or procedure receives its arguments through `:PARAMETERS`. Any
statement before it, including `:DECLARE`, is rejected, so the parameter list
is always the first statement after `:PROCEDURE` or at the top of a script.

rules.title: :DEFAULT immediately follows :PARAMETERS
rules.rule: `:DEFAULT` must immediately follow `:PARAMETERS`.
rules.rationale:
`:DEFAULT` lines supply a value for a parameter the caller left out. They are
only accepted directly after `:PARAMETERS`; zero or more may follow it, but no
other statement may come between.

rules.title: Call same-file procedures with DoProc
rules.rule: Use `DoProc("ProcName", {args})` for same-file script procedures.
rules.rationale:
A script procedure is not a function name the caller can use directly.
`DoProc` looks the name up in the current script, case-insensitively, and
passes the array's elements as the procedure's parameters.

rules.title: Call other scripts with ExecFunction
rules.rule: Use `ExecFunction("Category.Script", {args})` or `ExecFunction("Category.Script.Proc", {args})` for external script entry points.
rules.rationale:
A deployed script is addressed by its category and script name. The
two-segment form runs the script's top-level code; the three-segment form runs
one procedure in it. The array's elements become the target's parameters.

rules.title: No direct calls to custom procedures
rules.rule: Do not call custom script procedures directly as `MyProc()`.
rules.rationale:
A bare `Name(...)` call always means a built-in function. A name that is not
a built-in stops the script from compiling with
`Invalid built-in function: Name`, even when a procedure with that name is
declared in the same file.

rules.title: No :DEFAULT on a :DECLARE line
rules.rule: Do not put `:DEFAULT` on a `:DECLARE` line.
rules.rationale:
`:DEFAULT` belongs to parameters, not to local variables. A local declared
with `:DECLARE` starts empty; assign it a value in a separate statement.

rules.title: Declare locals at the start
rules.rule: Declare locals at the start of the script or procedure; this is a style preference, because `:DECLARE` is valid anywhere a statement is.
rules.rationale:
Declaring every local in one place shows the procedure's state before its
logic. The language does not require it: `:DECLARE` is an ordinary statement,
so a review reports a late declaration as a suggestion, not an error.

rules.title: Document every nontrivial procedure
rules.rule: Document every nontrivial local procedure with a doc block that states its purpose, its parameters, and what it returns.
rules.rationale:
A procedure's caller needs its contract without reading its body: what it
is for, what each parameter means, and what it gives back on success and on
failure.

rules.title: One physical line per Returns entry
rules.rule: Keep each `Returns:` entry of a procedure doc block on one physical line, for hover documentation.
rules.rationale:
Editors show the `Returns:` line when hovering over a call. A wrapped entry
shows only its first part.

good.code: * Returns: aResult - {.T., operation state} or failure envelope

bad.code:
* Returns: aResult - {.T., operation state}
 *          or failure envelope

rules.title: Prefer procedures without access modifiers
rules.rule: Prefer procedures without `/*@private;` or `/*@protected;` annotations; the one required exception is a raise-only helper, which is marked `/*@private;`.
rules.rationale:
An annotation blocks calls from other scripts. Most procedures do not need
that, and an unneeded one blocks a legitimate caller later. A raise-only
helper is the exception (see `private_raise_only_helpers`).

rules.title: Raise-only helpers are /*@private;
rules.rule: Mark raise-only helper procedures `/*@private;` so callers cannot bypass the entry point that catches their errors.
rules.rationale:
A helper that reports failure only by raising is safe only when called from
the entry point whose `:CATCH` turns the error into a result. `/*@private;`
blocks calls from other scripts, so no caller can reach the helper without
that boundary.

rules.title: An access modifier sits immediately before :PROCEDURE
rules.rule: Put an access modifier on its own line immediately before `:PROCEDURE`, with no blank line between them.
rules.rationale:
The modifier attaches to the `:PROCEDURE` that follows it directly. Separated
from it, it is an ordinary comment and the procedure stays callable from
other scripts.

rules.title: Access modifiers are written exactly
rules.rule: Write an access modifier exactly as `/*@private;` or `/*@protected;`: lowercase, with no space between `/*` and `@`.
rules.rationale:
Any other spelling is an ordinary comment. The procedure stays public, and
nothing reports that the modifier did not apply.

rules.title: No :PARAMETERS without parameters
rules.rule: Leave out `:PARAMETERS` and `:DEFAULT` when a procedure or method takes no parameters.
rules.rationale:
A procedure with no `:PARAMETERS` line takes no arguments; an empty
declaration adds nothing a reader needs.

rules.title: Align doc-block parameters only when it helps
rules.rule: Align parameter descriptions in a procedure doc block when it improves scanning, but do not force large spacing or fragile visual columns.
rules.rationale:
Aligned short names scan well. Columns padded to fit a long name push
descriptions far right and break on the next rename.

rules.title: Group declarations by purpose
rules.rule: Separate local variables with distinct responsibilities or lifecycles into purpose-based `:DECLARE` groups, such as request construction, configuration, retry state, response processing, transaction state and diagnostics.
rules.rationale:
A group per concern shows what state a procedure keeps and where each piece
belongs.

rules.title: Keep existing declaration groups
rules.rule: Preserve intentional declaration groups when editing existing code; do not flatten semantic groups into one declaration or reorganize all variables solely by type or prefix.
rules.rationale:
The groups record which state belongs together. Flattening them throws that
away and turns a small edit into a large diff.

rules.title: Order within a declaration group
rules.rule: Within each purpose-based `:DECLARE` group, order variables by prefix, then name; keep a single group only when the locals genuinely share one cohesive purpose.
rules.rationale: A fixed order inside a group makes a missing or duplicate name easy to spot.

rules.title: Read a global without declaring it
rules.rule: Read a predefined global by its name, without declaring it; a `:DECLARE`, `:PARAMETERS` entry or caller variable with the same name hides the global.
rules.rationale:
Globals are `:PUBLIC` variables, and publics are found last in variable
lookup. Declaring the name creates a local that hides the global, so the code
reads an empty string instead.

rules.title: Never assign to a global
rules.rule: Never assign to a global; nothing makes it read-only, and every routine that reads it afterwards sees your value.
rules.rationale:
A global is shared by everything that runs after the assignment, so changing
it changes their behavior too.

rules.title: Do not read globals a base installation lacks
rules.rule: Do not read a name the base installation does not declare (`CR`, `LF`, `TAB`, `sDQ`, `MYUSERID`, ...); use `Chr(...)` or the documented global instead, and guard a name that only some installations declare with `IsDefined("<name>")`.
rules.rationale:
Reading an undeclared name raises `Variable [<name>] is undefined!` where it
is missing, so code that works on one installation fails on another.

rules.title: Prefer :TRY over legacy :ERROR/:RESUME
rules.rule: Prefer `:TRY`/`:CATCH`/`:FINALLY` over legacy `:ERROR`/`:RESUME`.
rules.rationale:
`:ERROR`/`:RESUME` handlers still run, but they cover the whole procedure and,
in resume mode, run once for every failing statement. A `:TRY` block covers
only the statements that need it and has a `:FINALLY` for cleanup.

rules.title: :TRY needs :CATCH or :FINALLY
rules.rule: `:TRY` requires at least one of `:CATCH` or `:FINALLY`; a bare `:TRY ... :ENDTRY` is invalid.
rules.rationale:
The valid forms are `:TRY ... :CATCH ... :ENDTRY`,
`:TRY ... :FINALLY ... :ENDTRY` and `:TRY ... :CATCH ... :FINALLY ... :ENDTRY`.
A `:TRY` block with neither handler is rejected.

rules.title: UsrMes, ErrorMes and InfoMes write the server log
rules.rule: Do not assume `UsrMes`, `ErrorMes`, or `InfoMes` displays messages to users; they are server log functions.
rules.rationale:
Server scripts have no user interface. These functions write to the server
log; a message meant for the user goes back to the caller in the script's
result.

rules.title: One :CATCH per :TRY
rules.rule: Only one `:CATCH` block is allowed per `:TRY`; there is no multi-catch.
rules.rationale:
`:CATCH` does not name an exception type, so there is nothing to choose
between two handlers. Branch inside the one `:CATCH` on what
`GetLastSSLError()` returns.

rules.title: :CATCH comes before :FINALLY
rules.rule: When a `:TRY` has both handlers, `:CATCH` must precede `:FINALLY`.
rules.rationale:
The block reads in the order it runs: the protected statements, then the
handler for an error, then the cleanup that always runs.

rules.title: :TRY and :FINALLY bodies are not empty
rules.rule: The `:TRY` body requires at least one statement, and so does a `:FINALLY` body; a `:CATCH` body may be empty.

rules.title: Do not mix :ERROR and :TRY in one procedure
rules.rule: Do not combine legacy `:ERROR`/`:RESUME` handling with `:TRY`/`:CATCH` in the same procedure.
rules.rationale:
An `:ERROR` handler protects every statement before it, including any `:TRY`
block. In resume mode it takes an error raised inside the `:TRY` body before
`:CATCH` sees it, so `:CATCH` never runs and execution continues inside the
`:TRY` body.

rules.title: :ERROR is the last section and has a body
rules.rule: A legacy `:ERROR` handler is the last section of a procedure: it protects the statements before it, and its handler body needs at least one statement.
rules.rationale:
`:ERROR` runs to `:ENDPROC` and protects only what precedes it, so a handler
placed first protects nothing. An empty handler silently swallows every error
in the procedure.

rules.title: Raise inside the :TRY that handles it
rules.rule: Place `RaiseError` directly inside the `:TRY` block whose `:CATCH` handles it, so the raise can never escape.
rules.rationale:
`RaiseError` does not return. Inside `:TRY` it skips the rest of the
protected statements and hands control to `:CATCH`; execution then continues
after `:ENDTRY`. Raised anywhere else, the error travels up the call stack
until something catches it.
rules.exceptions:
A raise-only helper marked `/*@private;` raises outside any `:TRY`; its
caller's `:TRY` is the handling block (see `private_raise_only_helpers`).

rules.title: Never raise inside :CATCH
rules.rule: Never call `RaiseError` inside `:CATCH` — the error handler must not become the thing that crashes.
rules.rationale:
A raise inside `:CATCH` is not caught by that `:TRY`; it escapes to the
caller, so the handler that was meant to contain a failure becomes the source
of one. Return the failure from `:CATCH` instead.

rules.title: Every raise has a handler up the call stack
rules.rule: Every raise needs a `:TRY`/`:CATCH` (or legacy `:ERROR`/`:RESUME`) boundary somewhere up the call stack; an uncaught error fails the invocation and surfaces to the end user as a server error.
rules.rationale:
An error that no caller catches ends the whole invocation, and the end user
sees a server error instead of the failure the script was meant to report.
The entry point a caller reaches is where errors are turned into a result.

rules.title: Clear the error state after handling it
rules.rule: Call `ClearLastSSLError()` after handling an error in `:CATCH`, so stale error state does not leak into later handling.
rules.rationale:
The last error stays set after `:CATCH` finishes. Code that checks it later
would see the old failure as if it were new. Clear it once the handler has
read or dealt with it, never before.

rules.title: Read the error before changing the error state
rules.rule: In a `:CATCH` that keeps or logs diagnostics, read `GetLastSSLError()` before anything changes the SSL error state.
rules.rationale:
A call that clears or replaces the last error, including another call that
fails, leaves `GetLastSSLError()` describing something else. Capture the
error object first, then log, translate or clear it.

rules.title: Bound retained diagnostic text
rules.rule: Bound diagnostic text that a `:CATCH` keeps or logs, normally with `Left(..., 2000)`.
rules.rationale:
Full error descriptions can include stack details and nested causes and grow
without limit. A bounded copy keeps logs and result fields a predictable
size.

rules.title: Log a failure once, where it is owned
rules.rule: Log a diagnostic only at the boundary that owns the failed operation.
rules.rationale:
When every layer logs the same failure, one error becomes several log entries
with less context each. The boundary that owns the operation knows what was
being attempted; callers translate or propagate its result.

good.code:
WriteStatus (owns the write)  -> logs the diagnostic, returns {.F., {code, message}}
ChangeStatus (caller)         -> propagates the envelope, does not log again

bad.code:
WriteStatus   -> logs the diagnostic, returns a failure envelope
ChangeStatus  -> logs the same failure again
Main          -> logs it a third time

rules.title: Do not swallow errors silently
rules.rule: Log errors with contextual identifiers; avoid swallowing errors silently.
rules.rationale:
A `:CATCH` that neither logs, returns a failure, nor records the error hides
it: the operation looks successful to its caller and leaves nothing to
investigate. Include the identifiers that say which record or request failed.
rules.exceptions:
A boundary that turns the error into a stable failure result, or that
deliberately delegates logging to its caller, has not swallowed it.

rules.title: Wrap ExecFunction when you promise a failure envelope
rules.rule: When the current boundary promises a stable failure envelope, wrap `ExecFunction` in `:TRY`/`:CATCH` unless the deployed function has a documented no-throw contract, and validate the returned envelope even when the call is wrapped.
rules.rationale:
A deployed script can fail by raising, by returning a failure envelope, or
both. A boundary that promises callers an envelope has to catch the raise and
still check what a successful call returned.

rules.title: Validate a result before reading its payload
rules.rule: At every procedure or service boundary, validate an outer array, its required length and its success flag before reading an envelope payload, and validate the payload's shape and field types before indexing arrays or accessing object properties.
rules.rationale:
Indexing a value that is not an array, or reading a property an object does
not have, raises at run time. Checking the shape first turns a malformed
result into a handled contract failure instead of an error deep in the
caller.

rules.title: Keep valid downstream failures, replace malformed ones
rules.rule: When propagating a failure envelope, preserve a valid downstream stable code and sanitized message, and replace a malformed downstream result with a stable contract-failure code owned by the caller.
rules.rationale:
A valid downstream code already says what went wrong, and replacing it hides
that from the caller. A malformed result has no code to keep, so the caller
names the broken contract with a code of its own.

rules.title: Caller-safe failures carry a code and a sanitized message
rules.rule: Never return raw SSL diagnostics, exception descriptions, credentials, or payload bodies through caller-safe failures; return a stable code and a sanitized message.
rules.rationale:
Error descriptions can contain SQL text, file paths, connection details and
record contents. A caller needs a code it can branch on and a message it can
show; the diagnostic belongs in the server log.

rules.title: {.T., NIL} for a step with no success data
rules.rule: Use `{.T., NIL}` for internal command steps that use a standard envelope but have no success data.
rules.rationale:
One success shape for every data-less step keeps the caller's envelope check
the same everywhere: test the flag, and read the payload only when there is
one.

rules.title: Each invariant has one owning boundary
rules.rule: Assign each invariant to one authoritative boundary; repeat a check downstream only when it protects a distinct local use, enforces a stronger invariant, receives independently supplied data, or defends an independently deployed public contract.
rules.rationale:
The same check repeated at every layer adds code without adding safety, and
the copies drift apart. A check belongs where the value first becomes
trustworthy; later layers rely on that contract unless they have their own
reason to check.

good.code:
Main validates sSampleId once, then passes it to LoadSample and WriteStatus.
WriteStatus checks LimsRecordsAffected() == 1 (its own mutation guard).

bad.code: Main, LoadSample and WriteStatus each re-check that sSampleId is non-empty.

rules.title: One failure contract per pipeline
rules.rule: Use a pipeline-specific failure-capture helper when several sequential steps return standard envelopes, and keep one contract within the pipeline: either return a boolean or return `{success, state}` consistently.
rules.rationale:
One helper and one contract mean each step is checked the same way, and the
first failure is captured once.

rules.title: Comments explain why, not what
rules.rule: Comments explain purpose, ownership, safety consequences, replay behavior, or a non-obvious ordering requirement; do not narrate assignments or restate syntax.
rules.rationale:
The code already says what it does. A comment earns its place by saying what
the code cannot: why this order, who owns this state, what breaks if it
changes.

rules.title: Keep an expression on one line when it fits
rules.rule: Keep calls, assignments, conditions and other expressions on one physical line when they fit and remain readable; wrap only when the established line-length limit requires it or the split exposes meaningful structure.
rules.rationale:
An expression that fits on one line reads as one thing; breaking it without a
reason makes the reader rebuild it.

good.code:
:DECLARE sMessage;

sMessage := "Loaded " + LimsString(3) + " rows";

rules.title: Align the hanging lines of a wrapped list
rules.rule: When a declaration or similar comma-separated statement wraps, indent each hanging line so its first item aligns with the first item after the keyword.
rules.rationale:
Aligned items read as one list, and the hanging lines do not look like
statements of their own. The alignment is the statement's indent followed by
spaces, so it holds at any tab width.

rules.title: Continuation lines inside brackets align with the first item
rules.rule: Inside an unclosed `(`, `{` or `[` whose first item shares the bracket's line, align each continuation line with that first item (the opening line's indentation, then spaces); a bracket that ends its line hangs, with its items one level in and a leading closing delimiter back at the opening line's indentation; when an item would not fit at the aligned column, break right after the bracket and hang its items.
rules.rationale:
Aligned items show which bracket they belong to, so a reader sees the
argument or element structure without counting delimiters. A bracket that
ends its line has no first item to align with, so its items hang one level
in and the closing delimiter lines up with the line that opened it. The
alignment is the line's own indent followed by spaces, so it holds at any
tab width.

rules.title: Continuation indent shows the structure
rules.rule: Indent continuations to reveal expression or argument structure: outside brackets, one level past the line that opened the statement; inside a bracket, as `bracket_contents_align` says. Do not copy incidental alignment columns from another file.
rules.rationale:
The indent of a continuation line tells the reader which part of the
expression it belongs to; a column copied from elsewhere tells them nothing.

rules.title: A short envelope stays on one line
rules.rule: Keep a variable-only envelope such as `{.F., {sCode, sMessage}}` on one physical line when it fits.
rules.rationale:
A short envelope is easier to read as one value than spread over several
lines.
rules.exceptions:
Split an envelope when inline literal text, more payload fields or the
line-length limit benefit from clearer grouping.

rules.title: LimsTypeEx returns "NUMERIC", never "NUMBER"
rules.rule: Check numeric values against `"NUMERIC"` only; `LimsTypeEx` never returns `"NUMBER"`.
rules.rationale:
`LimsTypeEx` returns `NIL`, `STRING`, `NUMERIC`, `LOGIC`, `DATE`, `ARRAY`,
`CODEBLOCK`, `OBJECT` or `SSLVALUE`. A comparison with `"NUMBER"` is never
true, so the check it guards never runs.

rules.title: Check the type before the value
rules.rule: Separate runtime-type validation from value validation when `Len`, `Round`, array indexing or property access requires a specific type, and reject an invalid shape before evaluating the corresponding content predicate.
rules.rationale:
A content check such as `Len(v) > 0` raises when `v` has the wrong type, so
the type check has to come first.

rules.title: ErrorMes for messages that must always be logged
rules.rule: Use `ErrorMes` for messages that must be written even when normal user-message logging is disabled.
rules.rationale:
`UsrMes` output depends on the user-message logging setting. A failure that
someone must be able to investigate later is written with `ErrorMes`, which
does not.

rules.title: No secrets in logs
rules.rule: Avoid logging secrets, connection strings, passwords, or tokens.
rules.rationale:
Server logs are read by more people, and kept longer, than the systems the
secrets protect. A value written to a log has to be treated as disclosed.

rules.title: Logging is not error handling
rules.rule: Do not use logging as error handling when caller-visible behavior depends on the result.
rules.rationale:
A log entry tells an operator what happened; it tells the caller nothing.
When the caller's next step depends on whether the operation worked, the
failure has to be in the result.

rules.title: Tag log captions
rules.rule: Use `InfoMes` and `ErrorMes` for retained server-log diagnostics, and prefix captions with scan-friendly tags such as `[INFO]`, `[SUCCESS]`, or `[ERROR]`.
rules.rationale:
A shared server log mixes output from many scripts. A fixed tag at the start
of each caption makes the entries easy to filter and scan.

rules.title: Expected rejections are not infrastructure errors
rules.rule: Do not log expected guard rejections, replay conflicts, or caller validation failures as infrastructure errors unless the operation specifically requires that audit signal.
rules.rationale:
`[ERROR]` entries are what operators search for when something breaks. A
caller sending an invalid request is normal operation; logging it as an error
buries the real failures.

rules.title: Place :INCLUDE early
rules.rule: Place `:INCLUDE` early — it textually includes the referenced source before the script runs.
rules.rationale:
The included script is pasted in full, so everything it declares is in scope
for the rest of the file. Placing it after `:PARAMETERS` and `:DEFAULT` and
before other statements makes that visible to a reader.

rules.title: Conventional script declaration order
rules.rule: Recommended script order is `:PARAMETERS`, `:DEFAULT`, `:INCLUDE`, `:PUBLIC`, `:DECLARE`.
rules.rationale:
Only the first two positions are required by the language. The rest is a
convention that puts what the script receives, then what it pulls in, then
what it shares, then its own locals, in the same place in every file.

rules.title: Server script file shape
rules.rule: Order a nontrivial server script as: file banner; top-level `:PARAMETERS`, contiguous `:DEFAULT` statements and `:DECLARE`; default state initialization; main orchestration; then local procedures grouped into responsibility-based regions.
rules.rationale:
A reader finds the contract (banner and parameters) first, then the business
flow, and only then the helpers that implement it.
rules.exceptions: A short script with no local procedures needs no regions.

rules.title: Regions group related procedures
rules.rule: Use regions for meaningful groups of related procedures; do not create one region per procedure.
rules.rationale:
A region earns its place by folding away a responsibility a reader can skip.
One region per procedure only adds a pair of comment lines around each
procedure.

good.code:
/* region Request validation;   BuildRequest, ValidateRoute
/* region Status writes;        WriteStatus, WriteAudit

rules.title: Every server script and class file has a banner
rules.rule: Open every server script and class file with the standard file banner, using the dot-leader fields `Description`, `Parameters`, `Returns`, `Author` and `Date`.
rules.rationale:
The banner is the file's contract: what it does, what each parameter means,
and the exact result shape. Callers and reviewers read it before the code.
rules.exceptions:
Code generated by a tool or agent leaves out the `Author` line (see
`generated_banner_omits_author`).

rules.title: The banner states the exact result shape
rules.rule: State the exact result shape on the banner's `Returns......` line; when a script returns an outer envelope, describe the success and failure payloads on separate aligned continuation lines.
rules.rationale:
A caller writes its envelope check from this line. "Returns an array" does not
say which element is the flag or what a failure carries.

good.code:
Returns...... : {.T., NIL} on success
                {.F., {sCode, sMessage}} on failure

bad.code: Returns...... : array

rules.title: Banner continuation lines align after the colon
rules.rule: Continuation lines align under the first character after `: `.
rules.rationale:
Aligned continuations keep each field's value in one column, so a multi-line
`Parameters` or `Returns` entry reads as one value.

good.code:
Parameters... : sSampleId - Sample to update
                sStatus   - New status value

bad.code:
Parameters... : sSampleId - Sample to update
    sStatus - New status value

rules.title: Record changes as new Modified lines
rules.rule: Record later changes as new lines below `Date`, in the same style: `Modified..... : YYYY-MM-DD ABC - <what changed and why>`.
rules.rationale:
The banner's dated entries are the file's change history. Rewriting an
earlier entry to describe current work loses that history; a new line keeps
it.

good.code:
Date......... : 2026-03-02
Modified..... : 2026-10-13 ABC - Return a failure envelope when the write fails

rules.title: Generated code omits the banner Author line
rules.rule: Code generated by a tool or agent omits the `Author` line rather than inventing initials. A banner without `Author` is complete in that case, and a review does not report it.
rules.rationale:
Initials record who is accountable for a change. Initials an agent invents
record nothing true, so the line is left out.

good.code:
Returns...... : {.T., NIL} on success
Date......... : 2026-10-13

bad.code:
Returns...... : {.T., NIL} on success
Author....... : AI
Date......... : 2026-10-13

rules.title: No semicolon inside the banner
rules.rule: The banner is one comment, so it ends at the first `;`. Never put `;` anywhere inside it.
rules.rationale:
An SSL comment runs from `/*` to the first `;`. A semicolon inside the
banner ends the comment there, and the rest of the banner is read as code.
See `no_semicolon_in_comment_text`, which now states this for every comment.

rules.title: Banner description is one sentence
