rules.rule: Describe the script's single responsibility in one concise sentence on the banner's `Description` line.
rules.rationale:
One sentence is enough to say what a script with one responsibility does;
needing more suggests it does more than one thing.

good.code: Description.. : Records a status change for one sample.

bad.code:
Description.. : Updates samples. Also writes audit rows, sends the
                notification email and refreshes the dashboard cache.

rules.title: Banner parameters state their business meaning
rules.rule: Define every banner parameter by its exact business meaning.
rules.rationale:
The banner is the caller's contract. A type alone says what to pass, not which
value.

good.code:
Parameters... : sSampleId - Sample to update
                sStatus   - New status value

bad.code:
Parameters... : sSampleId - string
                sStatus   - string

rules.title: Success and Failure labels when a Returns line wraps
rules.rule: Use `Success:` and `Failure:` labels on the banner's `Returns` line when either description must wrap, and align continuations under the first character after the label.
rules.rationale: Labels keep the two shapes apart once a description runs onto a second line.

rules.title: A special result comes first on the Returns line
rules.rule: Keep a special non-envelope result on its own `Returns` continuation line before the handled success and failure shapes.
rules.rationale:
A result that is not an envelope needs different handling, so it is listed
first, where a caller looks.

good.code:
Returns...... : NIL when the request is a replay of a completed one
                {.T., NIL} on success
                {.F., {sCode, sMessage}} on failure

bad.code:
Returns...... : {.T., NIL} on success, or NIL for a replay
                {.F., {sCode, sMessage}} on failure

rules.title: Banner descriptions stay operational
rules.rule: Keep banner descriptions operational; do not restate obvious properties of SSL or SQL.
rules.rationale:
The banner says what this script does for its callers; how SSL or SQL behave
in general is in the reference.

good.code: Description.. : Records a status change for one sample.

bad.code:
Description.. : Uses SQLExecute, which binds ?name? markers, to run an
                UPDATE statement.

rules.title: No credentials in code
rules.rule: Do not hard-code credentials, passwords or connection strings in SSL code.
rules.rationale:
A credential in source is copied with every copy of the script and cannot be
changed without changing the code.

rules.title: Validate untrusted code and procedure names
rules.rule: Do not execute code or procedure names derived from untrusted input without validation.
rules.rationale:
`ExecFunction`, `DoProc` and `ExecUdf` run whatever name or code they are
given, so an unchecked value from a caller decides what runs.

rules.title: RunDS binds parameter values by position
rules.rule: Invoke data sources with `RunDS("Category.DataSourceName", {values})`; values bind by position in `:PARAMETERS` order, not by name. `GetDSParameters` returns the parameter names in that order. Do not pass `{name, value}` pairs; each pair is bound whole to one parameter.
rules.rationale:
`RunDS` matches the values array to the data source's `:PARAMETERS`
declaration by position; it does not look at names. A `{name, value}` pair is
one array element, so it is bound whole to one parameter. Use
`GetDSParameters(sDsName)` to see the declaration order.
rules.exceptions:
Trailing values left out take their inline defaults, and extra values are
ignored.

good.code:
:DECLARE oResult;

oResult := RunDS("Samples.ByStatus", {"P", 25});

bad.code:
:DECLARE oResult;
oResult := RunDS("Samples.ByStatus", {{"sStatus", "P"}, {"nLimit", 25}});

rules.title: Data sources take defaults inline, not from :DEFAULT
rules.rule: Data source files use inline `:PARAMETERS` defaults with `:=` instead of separate `:DEFAULT` statements.
rules.rationale:
Data source files are preprocessed before they run. The builder rewrites the
inline form `:PARAMETERS p1 := val1, p2 := val2;` into
`:PARAMETERS p1, p2; :DEFAULT p1, val1; :DEFAULT p2, val2;` itself, so a
hand-written `:DEFAULT` does not belong in a data source. The `:=` form is the
required syntax there, so a reviewer must not flag it as incorrect.
rules.exceptions:
Ordinary server scripts and class files still use `:PARAMETERS` followed by
`:DEFAULT`. This rule applies to data source files only.

good.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A", nMaxRows := 100;

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?");

rules.title: Every data-source parameter has an inline default
rules.rule: Give every data-source parameter an inline `:=` default; a parameter without one makes the data source fail when it runs.
rules.rationale:
The data source builder needs a default for each parameter it rewrites. When
one is missing, the data source fails at run time with
`No default value for one or more parameters.`, even when the caller passes a
value for that parameter.

good.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A", nMaxRows := 100;

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?");

bad.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A", nMaxRows;

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?");

rules.title: No empty :PARAMETERS line in a data source
rules.rule: A data source that takes no parameters leaves the `:PARAMETERS` line out; an empty `:PARAMETERS;` is an error.
rules.rationale:
In a data source file, `:PARAMETERS;` with no names after it is an error. A
data source without parameters has nothing to declare, so the line is omitted
rather than left empty.

good.code: :RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = 'A'");

bad.code:
:PARAMETERS;

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = 'A'");

rules.title: Data sources do not follow the script layout
rules.rule: Do not apply normal script `:PARAMETERS`/`:DEFAULT` layout to data-source files.
rules.rationale:
Data source files have their own structure. An SSL data source is an optional
header comment, `:PARAMETERS` with inline defaults, then the SSL body. A SQL
data source is an optional header comment, optional builder directives,
optional `:PARAMETERS` with inline defaults, then the SQL query. The script
layout (a required file banner, `:PARAMETERS` followed by `:DEFAULT`, then
`:INCLUDE`, `:PUBLIC` and `:DECLARE`) does not apply, so refactoring or
reviewing a data source against it gives wrong results.

good.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A", nMaxRows := 100;

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?");

rules.title: SQL data-source bodies use @name placeholders
rules.rule: Reference SQL data-source parameters in the SQL body as `@name` placeholders, not `?name?` markers.
rules.rationale:
The SQL body of a SQL data source references `:PARAMETERS` values as `@name`
placeholders whose names match the declarations. Write `@name` whatever the
database platform: the builder adapts placeholders to the backend. The
`?name?` markers belong to SQL embedded in SSL strings (`SQLExecute`); they are
not substituted in a SQL data source.
rules.exceptions: Placeholders inside quoted SQL literals are not substituted, in either form.

rules.title: Every @name placeholder is declared in :PARAMETERS
rules.rule: Declare every `@name` placeholder of a SQL data-source body in `:PARAMETERS`; an undeclared one is not substituted and fails when the query executes.
rules.rationale:
Only names declared in `:PARAMETERS` are substituted into the SQL body. A
`@name` with no matching declaration, most often a typo of a declared name,
reaches the database unchanged and the query fails there.
rules.exceptions: A declared parameter that the body never references is harmless.

rules.title: SQL data sources use SQL comments
rules.rule: Use SQL comment syntax (`--` and `/* ... */`) in SQL data-source bodies, not the SSL comment form.
rules.rationale:
The body of a SQL data source is SQL. A comment is `--` to the end of the line,
or `/* ... */` closed by `*/`. The SSL form, `/*` closed by the first `;`, is
not part of this file type: an unterminated `/*` reaches the database as
malformed SQL and fails there.
rules.exceptions:
Semicolons inside SQL comments and inside quoted SQL literals (for example
`'all;msoffice->pdf'`) are content. Comments may appear anywhere, including a
banner before the builder directives. Optimizer-hint comments (`/*+ ... */`)
are kept as written.

rules.title: No stray semicolons in a SQL data source
rules.rule: In a SQL data source, a semicolon only ends a builder directive or `:PARAMETERS`; the body runs as one SQL command, so any other semicolon outside a comment or string literal is misplaced.
rules.rationale:
A SQL data source's body runs as one SQL command, so a semicolon that does not
end a builder directive or `:PARAMETERS` is a stray statement separator. The
server refuses the whole document:
`Invalid SQL statement: remove any misplaced semicolons(;)`. The common case is
a banner ended with `*/;`, which is correct in an SSL data source and wrong in
a SQL one. Other cases are a `;` on a line of its own, a doubled `;;`, and a
trailing `;` after the query.
rules.exceptions: Semicolons inside SQL comments and quoted SQL literals are content.

rules.title: The SQL body follows :PARAMETERS
rules.rule: In a SQL data source, put the SQL body after the `:PARAMETERS` line; SQL text placed before it is discarded.
rules.rationale:
The builder reads a SQL data source as a header (comments, builder directives
and `:PARAMETERS`) followed by the query. SQL text placed before
`:PARAMETERS` is discarded during preprocessing, so that part of the query
never runs.
rules.exceptions:
Builder directives and comments may come before `:PARAMETERS`. A SQL data
source with no parameters has no `:PARAMETERS` line, and its query follows the
directives.

rules.title: SQL data-source queries use the canonical compact layout
rules.rule: Lay out the query body of a SQL data source in the canonical compact SQL style, the same as SQL embedded in SSL strings.
rules.rationale:
The canonical compact reference defines one SQL layout for the repository.
Its scope note says the layout also applies to the query body of a SQL data
source, even though the file's header (builder directives and `:PARAMETERS`)
has its own structure.

good.code:
:DSN := DATABASE;
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A";

SELECT sampleid, status
FROM sample
WHERE status = @sStatus
  AND note <> 'x'
ORDER BY sampleid

rules.title: Builder directives are valid in SQL data sources
rules.rule: SQL data-source builder directives (`:DSN`, `:TABLENAME`, `:NULLASBLANK`, `:INVARIANTDATECOLUMNS`) are preprocessed before compilation and are not normal SSL keywords; do not flag them as unknown keywords.
rules.rationale:
`:DSN`, `:TABLENAME`, `:NULLASBLANK` and `:INVARIANTDATECOLUMNS` configure how
a SQL data source runs. The builder handles them before the data source runs,
so they are not part of the SSL keyword set. A reviewer or formatter must not
report them as unknown keywords, and must not remove them.

bad.code: Review finding on a SQL data source: ":DSN is not an SSL keyword - remove it."

rules.title: Builder directives exist only in SQL data sources
rules.rule: Do not treat builder directives as reusable SSL keywords outside data-source contexts.
rules.rationale:
`:DSN`, `:TABLENAME`, `:NULLASBLANK` and `:INVARIANTDATECOLUMNS` are read by the
SQL data source builder. They are not SSL keywords, so in a server script or a
class file they are errors. To get data through a data source from a
script, call the data source with `RunDS`.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := RunDS("Samples.ByStatus", {"A"});

rules.title: SSL data sources use SSL comments
rules.rule: In an SSL data source, comments are SSL comments: they end at the first `;`, and `*/` does not close them.
rules.rationale:
The body of an SSL data source is SSL, so the SSL comment rules apply
throughout, including the optional header comment. A `*/` there is ordinary
comment text: a comment that ends with `*/` and no `;` runs on and swallows
the statement after it, which then never runs while still reading as live
code. `*/;` is correct in an SSL data source and wrong in a SQL one (see
datasource_sql_semicolon).

rules.title: SSL data sources use parameters as variables
rules.rule: In an SSL data source, use parameters as ordinary variables by their bare names; `@name` placeholders are not part of this file type.
rules.rationale:
The body of an SSL data source is an SSL script. Its parameters are variables,
so embedded SQL references them the way any script does, for example as
`?name?` markers in `SQLExecute`. A `@name` written into a `SQLExecute`
string is not substituted.
rules.exceptions:
`GetSSLDataset` uses `@name` markers with parallel name and value arrays as
part of its own call syntax, for example
`GetSSLDataset("SELECT * FROM sample WHERE status = @sStatus",, {"@sStatus"}, {sStatus})`.
That is the function's syntax, not a data-source placeholder.

good.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A";

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?");

bad.code:
:PARAMETERS sStatus := "A";

:RETURN SQLExecute("SELECT sample_id FROM sample WHERE status = @sStatus");

rules.title: RunDS return types convert only an SSLDataset
rules.rule: The `RunDS` return-type argument (`"ssldataset"`, `"xml"`, and so on) converts only an `SSLDataset` result; an SSL data source that callers request in another return type returns an `SSLDataset`, for example from `GetSSLDataset`.
rules.rationale:
`RunDS` converts the data source's result to the requested return type only
when that result is an `SSLDataset`. An SSL data source whose body returns an
array, for example from `SQLExecute`, returns that array whatever return type
the caller asks for.

rules.title: A file is a class, a script or a data source
rules.rule: One file should represent either a class definition, a script, or a data source.
rules.rationale:
Each file kind has its own structure and is run differently: a class file is
instantiated, a script is called, and a data source is preprocessed and then
run through `RunDS`. Mixing kinds in one file breaks the structure of each.

rules.title: Bind values with placeholders, never concatenate them into SQL
rules.rule: Prefer parameterized database calls; do not concatenate user or runtime values into SQL when placeholders can bind them.
rules.rationale:
A value concatenated into SQL text becomes part of the statement, so a quote
in the value changes what the statement does. A placeholder passes the value
separately and the database never parses it as SQL. Placeholders also keep the
statement text stable, which the formatter and the parameter checks rely on.
rules.exceptions:
Fixed fragments chosen by the code itself (a column name picked from a closed
list, for example) are not values and may be concatenated. Never concatenate
anything a user or another system supplied.

rules.title: Only SQLExecute substitutes ?name? markers
rules.rule: `SQLExecute` is the only database API that supports named `?param?` substitution; do not use `?param?` markers with other database functions. Its markers reference in-scope SSL variables by name. Canonical shape: `SQLExecute("UPDATE T SET COL = ?sValue? WHERE ID = ?nId?");`
rules.rationale:
`SQLExecute` reads each `?name?` marker as an SSL expression, usually a
variable in scope, and substitutes its value. The other database functions
treat `?` as a positional marker and bind values from an array, so a
`?name?` marker reaches the database as text and the query fails. Because
`SQLExecute` takes its values from the markers, its second argument is a
connection name: an array passed there is not a values array.
rules.exceptions:
`GetSSLDataset` uses `@name` markers with name and value arrays (see
`getssldataset_at_name_markers`).

rules.title: Other database functions bind positional ? markers from a values array
rules.rule: `RunSQL`, `LSearch`, `LSelect`, `LSelect1`, `LSelectC`, and `GetDataSet` use positional `?` markers with a value array in a later argument slot: fourth for `LSearch`, `LSelect` and `LSelectC`, second for `GetDataSet`, and third for `RunSQL` and `LSelect1`. Check `ssl_signature` for the slot and skip unused optionals with adjacent commas. Canonical shape: `aRows := LSelect("SELECT ID FROM T WHERE STATUS = ?",,, {sStatus});`
rules.rationale:
Each function takes its values array at a fixed argument position, after
optional arguments such as a connection name or a default value. An array
passed in an earlier slot is read as that earlier argument: for `LSelect` the
second slot is an unimplemented field list, and any value there raises an
error. Skipped optionals are written as adjacent commas, not `NIL`.

rules.title: GetSSLDataset binds @name markers from name and value arrays
rules.rule: `GetSSLDataset` uses `@name` markers with parallel name and value arrays.
rules.rationale:
`GetSSLDataset(sSql, [sDsn], [aParamNames], [aParamValues], ...)` matches each
`@name` in the SQL text to the same name in the names array and binds the
value at the same index of the values array. It does not read `?` or `?name?`
markers.

rules.title: Omit a trailing empty optional array
rules.rule: Do not pass empty trailing optional parameters when they can be omitted.
rules.rationale:
A trailing `{}` for an optional parameter changes nothing; the call works the
same without it. Leaving it out keeps the call short and makes a values array
that is actually passed stand out.
rules.exceptions:
An empty array followed by further arguments is a positional placeholder and
stays.

good.code:
:DECLARE sXml;

sXml := GetDataSet("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask");

bad.code:
:DECLARE sXml;
sXml := GetDataSet("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask", {});

rules.title: SQLExecute takes no values array
rules.rule: A values array on `SQLExecute`: `SQLExecute(sSql, {args})` passes the array as a **connection name** — SQLExecute binds via `?name?` markers only (see the database rules above).
rules.rationale:
`SQLExecute` takes its values from the `?name?` markers in the SQL text. Its
second parameter is a connection name, so an array passed there is not bound
to anything.

rules.title: Expand only a local array in IN
rules.rule: Expand only a local array in `IN (?aValues?)`: a UDObject array property expanded directly raises a runtime error, so copy it to a local first.
rules.rationale:
`SQLExecute` expands a local array into one bound value per element. An array
reached through a UDObject property fails with "The current array has more
than 1 dimmension." when it runs.
rules.exceptions: A scalar property such as `?oUser:ID?` binds normally.

rules.title: RunSQL is for statements that return no rows
rules.rule: Use `RunSQL` for statements that return no rows (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, DDL), inside `:TRY`/`:CATCH`.
rules.rationale:
`RunSQL` reports whether the statement ran and discards any rows, so a query
needs a result-returning function such as `LSearch`, `LSelect` or
`SQLExecute`.

rules.title: LSearch for single-value lookups
rules.rule: Use `LSearch` for single-value lookups, with explicit parameters.
rules.rationale:
`LSearch` returns the first column of the first row directly, so a lookup
needs no result array to unpack.

rules.title: Copy object properties into locals for SQL
rules.rule: Copy object properties into typed locals before embedding them in SQL.
rules.rationale:
A typed local names the value the query binds, and its prefix says what type
the placeholder receives.

rules.title: Decide what an empty IN array means
rules.rule: When the array for an `IN (?aValues?)` predicate is empty, skip that query or choose the appropriate fallback.
rules.rationale:
An empty selection can mean "no rows" or "no filter". The query cannot tell
which, so the code decides before it runs.

rules.title: No connection argument for the default database
rules.rule: Omit the connection argument for calls to the default database.
rules.rationale:
The default database is what a call without a connection argument uses, so
naming it adds an argument that can only go stale.
rules.exceptions: A call to a named connection passes that connection.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask", "DEFAULT");

rules.title: Check the rows a guarded write changed
rules.rule: For guarded writes, require `LimsRecordsAffected() == 1`, and perform a verification read when later logic depends on the resulting state or state version.
rules.rationale:
A guarded `UPDATE` that matches no row succeeds without changing anything.
Only the affected-row count tells the command that its guard did not hold.

rules.title: Non-trivial queries are multi-line strings, one major clause per line
rules.rule: Use multiline SQL strings for non-trivial queries and put major clauses on separate lines.
rules.rationale:
A query laid out one clause per line can be read, compared and reviewed
clause by clause. The formatter keeps a multi-line string in the canonical
compact layout, but leaves a single-line string that fits its line exactly as
written.
rules.exceptions: A short, simple lookup (one table, one condition) may stay on one line.

rules.title: The SQL block sits 4 spaces inside the string
rules.rule: Indent the whole SQL block 4 spaces inside the SSL string literal.
rules.rationale:
The 4-space indent sets the SQL off from the SSL statement around it. Every
other SQL indent (clauses at 0, sub-clauses at 2) is measured from it.

rules.title: Major clauses start at column 0 of the SQL block
rules.rule: Start each major clause at column 0 relative to the 4-space indent: `SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT OUTER JOIN`, `RIGHT OUTER JOIN`, `FULL OUTER JOIN`, `CROSS JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, `UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `INTERSECT`, `MINUS`, `INSERT INTO`, `VALUES`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE FROM`, `MERGE INTO`, `USING`, `WHEN MATCHED THEN`, `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN`, `START WITH`, `CONNECT BY`, `PIVOT`, `UNPIVOT`, `FOR UPDATE`, `RETURNING`.
rules.rationale:
Clauses at a fixed column make a query's shape visible at a glance: each line
that starts at column 0 begins a new clause, and everything indented belongs
to the clause above it.

rules.title: SQL lines target about 90 characters
rules.rule: Keep SQL lines to about 90 characters, breaking at logical points.
rules.rationale:
About 90 characters fits a side-by-side diff and a review pane without
wrapping. Breaking at clause and list boundaries keeps each line meaningful
on its own.
rules.exceptions:
A single token that cannot fit, such as a long string literal, leaves its line
over-long; tokens are never split.

rules.title: SQL list commas trail the line
rules.rule: Put commas at the end of the line (trailing comma style), not at the start of the next line.
rules.rationale:
Trailing commas keep each continuation line starting with a column, so a
packed `SELECT` list reads left to right like prose.

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno
         , testcode
         , status
    FROM ordtask
");

rules.title: Pre-compute values instead of computing them inside ?name? markers
rules.rule: Pre-compute complex values before interpolating them into `SQLExecute` placeholders.
rules.rationale:
`SQLExecute` evaluates the expression inside each `?...?` marker every time
the statement runs. A plain variable is cheaper, easier to read, and holds a
value you can inspect before the query runs.

rules.title: Build dynamic IN clauses from arrays, not by hand
rules.rule: Use `PrepareArrayForIn` or `SQLExecute` array expansion for dynamic `IN` clauses when appropriate; do not build an `IN` clause by hand when a safer array helper or parameter array is available.
rules.rationale:
`SQLExecute` expands an array in an `IN (?aValues?)` marker into one bound
value per element, so the values never become SQL text. A hand-built list
concatenates values into the statement, with the same injection and quoting
problems as any other concatenation.
rules.exceptions:
Expand only a local variable. A UDObject array property used directly in the
marker raises a runtime error; copy it to a local first.

rules.title: SQL keywords and functions are uppercase
rules.rule: Inside SQL strings, write SQL keywords and built-in functions in uppercase.
rules.rationale:
Uppercase keywords separate the fixed SQL vocabulary from the table, column
and alias names around it, and from the mixed-case SSL code outside the
string.
rules.exceptions:
The formatter leaves a single-line query that fits its line exactly as
written, keyword case included, so fix such a query by hand.

rules.title: Preserve the author's identifier casing
rules.rule: Preserve the author's casing for table names, column names and aliases; force-folding is dialect-conditional (safe on Oracle, but breaks case-sensitive SQL Server collations), so lowercase only Oracle-only code.
rules.rationale:
On Oracle, unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive, so folding them is
safe. On SQL Server, identifier comparison follows the database collation, and
on a case-sensitive collation `RESULTS` and `results` name different objects.
A STARLIMS environment may run on either, so preserving the author's casing is
the only safe default. Double-quoted identifiers are never re-cased.
rules.exceptions:
Code that only ever runs on Oracle may lowercase identifiers; the formatter
setting `ssl.format.sql.identifierCase: lower` is that opt-in.

bad.code:
Author wrote:  SELECT SampleID, Status FROM Sample WHERE Status = ?sStatus?
Rewritten as:  SELECT sampleid, status FROM sample WHERE status = ?sStatus?
On a case-sensitive SQL Server collation the rewritten query names other objects.

rules.title: Keep the casing an external object requires
rules.rule: Preserve external schema or object casing when the schema or object requires it.
rules.rationale:
Some objects are created with a fixed casing: quoted identifiers, objects
owned by another system, or names on a case-sensitive collation. Their casing
is part of the name, so it survives even an Oracle-only lowercase pass.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute('SELECT "OrderNo", "Status" FROM "ExtOrders"');

bad.code:
Author wrote:  SELECT "OrderNo", "Status" FROM "ExtOrders"
Rewritten as:  SELECT "orderno", "status" FROM "extorders"
The quoted names no longer match the objects.

rules.title: AND/OR continue 2 spaces in, aligned with ON and HAVING
rules.rule: Start each `AND`/`OR` condition on its own line, indented 2 spaces under `WHERE`; in a join condition it aligns with `ON`, and in a `HAVING` condition with `HAVING`.
rules.rationale:
Major clauses sit at column 0 of the SQL block, so a 2-space step sets each
condition off from the next clause without spending a full indent level.
`ON` and `HAVING` already sit 2 in, so their conditions line up with them.

good.code:
:DECLARE sStatus, aRows;

sStatus := "Logged";
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno, t.testcode
    FROM orders o
    INNER JOIN ordtask t
      ON t.ordno = o.ordno
      AND t.testcode = 'PH'
    WHERE o.status = ?sStatus?
      AND t.status = 'Done'
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE sStatus, aRows;
sStatus := "Logged";
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno, t.testcode
    FROM orders o
    INNER JOIN ordtask t
      ON t.ordno = o.ordno
        AND t.testcode = 'PH'
    WHERE o.status = ?sStatus?
    AND t.status = 'Done'
");

rules.title: ON sits 2 spaces under its JOIN
rules.rule: Indent `ON` 2 spaces under its `JOIN` (in `MERGE`, `ON` stays at column 0).
rules.rationale:
A join condition belongs to its `JOIN`, so it indents under it like any other
sub-clause. In `MERGE`, `ON` is a clause of the statement itself and starts at
column 0 (see `sql_merge_layout`).

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno, t.testcode
    FROM orders o
    INNER JOIN ordtask t
      ON t.ordno = o.ordno
");

rules.title: HAVING sits 2 spaces under GROUP BY
rules.rule: Indent `HAVING` 2 spaces under `GROUP BY`.
rules.rationale:
This style treats `HAVING` as a sub-clause of `GROUP BY`: it filters the
groups that clause made. Styles that put `HAVING` at column 0 differ on
purpose.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno, COUNT(*) AS ntests
    FROM ordtask
    GROUP BY ordno
      HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno, COUNT(*) AS ntests
    FROM ordtask
    GROUP BY ordno
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
");

rules.title: A broken BETWEEN range aligns its AND under BETWEEN
rules.rule: When a `BETWEEN ... AND` range breaks across lines, align its `AND` under `BETWEEN`.
rules.rationale:
The `AND` of a range is not a condition separator. Aligning it under
`BETWEEN` keeps it from reading as the start of a new `AND` condition, which
sits 2 spaces in.

good.code:
WHERE o.logdate BETWEEN TO_DATE('2026-01-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD')
                AND TO_DATE('2026-12-31', 'YYYY-MM-DD')

bad.code:
WHERE o.logdate BETWEEN TO_DATE('2026-01-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD')
  AND TO_DATE('2026-12-31', 'YYYY-MM-DD')

rules.title: WHEN and ELSE indent under CASE
rules.rule: Indent `WHEN`/`ELSE` 4 spaces under `CASE`.
rules.rationale:
`WHEN` and `ELSE` belong to their `CASE`, so they indent one 4-space step
under it, and the branches line up as a table of conditions and results.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
               WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
               WHEN o.status = 'C' THEN 'Complete'
               ELSE 'Unknown'
           END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
             WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
             WHEN o.status = 'C' THEN 'Complete'
             ELSE 'Unknown'
           END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

rules.title: END aligns with its CASE
rules.rule: Align `END` with its `CASE`.
rules.rationale:
`END` closes the block that `CASE` opens. Putting it back at the `CASE`
column shows where the expression ends, and any alias after `END` reads as
belonging to the whole expression.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
               WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
               ELSE 'Unknown'
           END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
               WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
               ELSE 'Unknown'
               END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

rules.title: A CASE block keeps all branches inline or all broken
rules.rule: Within one `CASE` block, keep all `WHEN`/`THEN` branches inline or break them all; do not mix. `ELSE` may stay inline when its value is short.
rules.rationale:
A `CASE` whose branches share one shape reads as a table of conditions and
results. Mixing inline and broken branches hides which results belong to
which conditions.
rules.exceptions:
A short `ELSE` value may stay on the `ELSE` line even when the `WHEN`
branches are broken.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
               WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
               WHEN o.status = 'C' THEN 'Complete'
               ELSE 'Unknown'
           END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT o.ordno,
           CASE
               WHEN o.status = 'L' THEN 'Logged'
               WHEN o.status = 'C' THEN
                   'Complete'
               ELSE 'Unknown'
           END AS status_desc
    FROM orders o
");

rules.title: A broken THEN value indents under its WHEN
rules.rule: When a `THEN` value breaks to a new line, indent it 4 spaces under its `WHEN`.
rules.rationale:
A long result reads as part of its `WHEN` when it sits one step under it, and
the next `WHEN` still starts at the branch column.

good.code:
CASE
    WHEN status = 'Complete' AND result_value IS NOT NULL THEN
        ROUND(result_value / baseline_value * 100, 2)
    WHEN status = 'Complete' AND result_value IS NULL THEN
        0
    ELSE -1
END AS pct_of_baseline

bad.code:
CASE
    WHEN status = 'Complete' AND result_value IS NOT NULL THEN
    ROUND(result_value / baseline_value * 100, 2)
    WHEN status = 'Complete' AND result_value IS NULL THEN
    0
    ELSE -1
END AS pct_of_baseline

rules.title: Pack the SELECT list; give complex expressions their own line
rules.rule: Pack `SELECT` columns onto lines up to about 90 characters: short aliases (`col AS alias`) and simple functions (`COUNT(*)`, `UPPER(col)`) can share a line, and complex expressions (`CASE`, nested functions, subqueries) break to their own line.
rules.rationale:
A packed list keeps a wide query short enough to see whole, and a complex
expression on its own line is still easy to find and read.

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno,
           testcode,
           status AS task_status,
           UPPER(result) AS result_upper
    FROM ordtask
");

rules.title: SELECT continuation lines align to the first column
rules.rule: Align `SELECT` continuation lines to the first column (column 7).
rules.rationale:
`SELECT` plus a space is 7 characters, so column 7 is where the first column
name starts. Continuation lines that start there read as one list.

rules.title: INSERT column and VALUES lists use block-style parentheses
rules.rule: In `INSERT`, put the opening `(` on the `INSERT INTO` line, indent the columns 4 spaces, and put the closing `)` on its own line; lay out `VALUES` the same way.
rules.rationale:
Block-style parentheses keep the column list and the value list the same
shape, so the nth column and the nth value line up when you compare them.

rules.title: UPDATE keeps SET on its line and indents the assignments
rules.rule: In `UPDATE`, keep `SET` on the `UPDATE` line and indent the assignments 4 spaces below it.
rules.rationale:
One assignment per line, indented under `UPDATE ... SET`, makes the list of
changed columns easy to scan and to diff.

rules.title: Layout of an existing MERGE
rules.rule: When formatting an existing `MERGE`, put `ON` at column 0 (not indented under `USING`), indent the `AND` of a multi-line `ON` condition 4 spaces (under the first condition inside the parentheses), indent `UPDATE SET`, `INSERT` and `DELETE WHERE` 4 spaces under their `WHEN`, end the `UPDATE SET` line at `SET` with each assignment on its own line 4 spaces further in (as in a plain `UPDATE`), keep `DELETE WHERE` on one line with each `AND`/`OR` of its condition on its own line 4 spaces further in, and give the `INSERT` block-style parentheses.
rules.rationale:
In `MERGE`, `ON` is a clause of the statement, not of `USING`, so it starts
at column 0 like the other clauses. The actions under each `WHEN` indent one
level, the way `THEN` values do. `UPDATE SET` lays out like a plain `UPDATE`,
so each assignment is easy to see and to edit.
rules.exceptions:
Agents do not write `MERGE` (see `sql_basic_sql_only`). This layout is for
formatting `MERGE` statements that already exist.

good.code:
:DECLARE sOrdNo, sStatus;

sOrdNo := "A1001";
sStatus := "Done";
SQLExecute("
    MERGE INTO ordtask t
    USING (
        SELECT ?sOrdNo? AS ordno, ?sStatus? AS status
        FROM dual
    ) s
    ON (t.ordno = s.ordno
        AND t.status <> s.status
        AND t.department_code = s.department_code)
    WHEN MATCHED THEN
        UPDATE SET
            t.status = s.status,
            t.changed_on = SYSDATE
        DELETE WHERE t.status = 'Cancelled'
            AND t.changed_on < SYSDATE - 30
    WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
        INSERT (
            ordno, status
        )
        VALUES (
            s.ordno, s.status
        )
");

rules.title: Set operators stand between blank lines
rules.rule: Put a blank line before and after `UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `INTERSECT` and `MINUS`.
rules.rationale:
Each side of a set operation is a whole query. Blank lines around the
operator show where one query ends and the next begins.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno
    FROM ordtask
    WHERE status = 'Logged'

    UNION

    SELECT ordno
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'Open'
");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("
    SELECT ordno
    FROM ordtask
    WHERE status = 'Logged'
    UNION
    SELECT ordno
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'Open'
");

rules.title: Optimizer hints stay after their action keyword
rules.rule: Keep an optimizer hint (`/*+ HINT */`) immediately after its action keyword; never remove or reformat a hint without understanding its purpose.
rules.rationale:
A hint only works directly after `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or
`MERGE`; anywhere else it is an ordinary comment. Hints are usually there to
fix a measured performance problem, so removing one can bring that problem
back.

rules.title: One placeholder style per call
rules.rule: Do not mix named and positional placeholder mental models in the same call.
rules.rationale:
Each database function reads one placeholder shape: `?name?` for
`SQLExecute`, positional `?` with a values array for the others, and `@name`
for `GetSSLDataset`. A call that mixes shapes leaves some markers unbound.

rules.title: Embedded SQL has no trailing semicolon
rules.rule: Do not put a trailing semicolon inside an embedded SQL string — `"SELECT ... ;"` is not the convention; end the SSL statement, not the SQL text.
rules.rationale:
The SQL text in a database call carries no terminator. The semicolon that
ends the line belongs to the SSL statement; a second one inside the string
adds nothing the call needs.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask WHERE status = 'Logged'");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask WHERE status = 'Logged';");

rules.title: SQL written by agents stays basic
rules.rule: Keep SQL you write basic: plain `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` with ordinary joins, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `ORDER BY`. Do not write temp tables, table variables, CTEs, window functions, cursors, dynamic SQL assembled at runtime, `MERGE`, stored-procedure definitions, or control-flow blocks (`IF`, `WHILE`, `BEGIN…END`) inside a SQL string; when a result needs that shape, compute it in SSL across simpler queries.
rules.rationale:
STARLIMS struggles with programmatic SQL. Splitting a complex shape into
simple queries combined in SSL keeps each query easy to read, bind and check.
rules.exceptions:
Existing code may contain these constructs. Formatting or reviewing it is
fine; rewriting it is a separate decision.

rules.title: No N prefix unless Unicode is required
rules.rule: Use ordinary SQL string literals; add the `N` prefix only when the target explicitly requires Unicode literal semantics.
rules.rationale:
An `N'...'` literal changes the literal's type, which can change how a
comparison is evaluated against a non-Unicode column.

good.code:
:DECLARE aRows;

aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask WHERE status = 'Logged'");

bad.code:
:DECLARE aRows;
aRows := SQLExecute("SELECT ordno FROM ordtask WHERE status = N'Logged'");

rules.title: COLLATE only for a documented contract
rules.rule: Let ordinary text comparisons use the schema or database collation; force `COLLATE` only for a documented comparison contract, and explain why the schema collation is insufficient immediately before the query.
rules.rationale:
A forced collation overrides what the schema promises for that column. Without
the reason next to it, a reader cannot tell whether it is a contract or an
accident.

rules.title: SQL layout shows lock and guard conditions
rules.rule: Use structured SQL with clause-per-line formatting and indentation that exposes lock and guard conditions.
rules.rationale:
The guard and lock conditions decide whether a write is safe, so they belong
where a reviewer sees them, each on its own line.

rules.title: Lock hints follow the concurrency contract
rules.rule: Apply lock hints deliberately for the operation's concurrency contract.
rules.rationale:
A lock hint changes what concurrent commands can see and do. One added by
habit blocks other work; one left out lets two commands act on the same row.

rules.title: Class member order
rules.rule: Order class members as `:INHERIT`, then the class-level `:DECLARE` fields, then the methods.
rules.rationale:
`:INHERIT` names the parent before anything else, and the fields come before
the methods that use them, so a reader sees the object's shape before its
behavior.

rules.title: Constructor after the regular methods (convention)
rules.rule: By convention, declare `Constructor` after the regular methods, as the last method of the class; a class that declares it first compiles and runs the same way.
rules.rationale:
Keeping `Constructor` in one predictable place makes a class easy to scan.
The position has no effect on how the class compiles or runs, so an existing
class that declares `Constructor` first does not need reordering.

rules.title: Qualify class fields with Me or Base
rules.rule: Inside class methods, access fields through `Me:fieldName` or `Base:fieldName`.
rules.rationale:
A bare name inside a method follows normal variable lookup: local, then the
callers' scopes, then publics. It never reaches the field, so a bare write
leaves the field unchanged and a bare read can raise `Variable [name] is
undefined!`.

rules.title: Call class methods through Me and Base
rules.rule: Call sibling or inherited methods with `Me:Method()` and `Base:Method()`.
rules.rationale:
A method belongs to an instance. `Me:` calls it on the current instance, and
`Base:` calls the parent class's version.

rules.title: Instantiate user classes as Category.ClassName
rules.rule: Use `CreateUdObject("Category.ClassName")` for user-defined classes; a bare class name is looked up only among the default categories.
rules.rationale:
A class file is a script in a category. Without the category, the lookup
searches only the default categories and raises `There is no script with
name: <name> among default categories.` for a class in your own category.

rules.title: :INHERIT names the parent with its category
rules.rule: Write `:INHERIT` with the full `Category.ClassName` of the parent class; a plain class name is a compile-time error.
rules.rationale:
The parent is found by its full script name. A plain name fails when the class
compiles with `Specify the full name of the class in :INHERIT`.

rules.title: CreateUdObject is not for built-in classes
rules.rule: Do not instantiate built-in classes with `CreateUdObject`.
rules.rationale:
`CreateUdObject` creates dynamic objects and instances of user-defined
classes. A built-in class name passed to it is not found.

good.code:
:DECLARE oEmail;

oEmail := Email{};

bad.code:
:DECLARE oEmail;
oEmail := CreateUdObject("Email");

rules.title: One class per file
rules.rule: Define only one `:CLASS` per file.
rules.rationale:
A class runs from `:CLASS` to the end of the file, so a second `:CLASS` cannot
start inside it.

rules.title: A class ends at the end of the file
rules.rule: `:CLASS` continues to end of file; there is no `:ENDCLASS`.
rules.rationale: A class file holds exactly one class, so the end of the file ends the class.

rules.title: Name every class
rules.rule: Give every class an explicit name in `:CLASS`; the name is syntactically optional.
rules.rationale:
The name documents which class the file holds, for readers and for tools that
list classes.

rules.title: Class members stay at the top indentation level
rules.rule: Do not indent the class body because of `:CLASS`; class members stay at the file's top indentation level.
rules.rationale:
`:CLASS` opens no block; the class simply runs to the end of the file. The
formatter keeps members at the top level.

rules.title: A Constructor returns no value
rules.rule: `:RETURN` inside a `Constructor` cannot return a value.
rules.rationale:
`CreateUdObject` returns the new instance. A value returned from the
constructor has nowhere to go, so it is rejected.

rules.title: Constructor only inside a class
rules.rule: Use `Constructor` only inside a `:CLASS` definition.
rules.rationale:
`Constructor` is the reserved name of a class's constructor. In a script it is
an ordinary procedure name that nothing calls as a constructor.

rules.title: Call a parent Constructor that takes parameters
rules.rule: With `:INHERIT`, the parent's parameterless `Constructor` runs automatically first; a parent `Constructor` that takes parameters runs only if the derived `Constructor` calls `Base:Constructor(args)`.
rules.rationale:
A parent constructor that needs arguments cannot be called for you. Without
the explicit call, the parent's fields keep their declared empty values.

rules.title: Me only inside a class
rules.rule: Use `Me` only inside a `:CLASS` definition.
rules.rationale: `Me` is the current class instance. A script has no instance for it to name.
rules.exceptions: A library compiled into a class through `:INCLUDE` may use `Me`.

rules.title: Base needs :INHERIT and a member
rules.rule: Use `Base` only in a class with `:INHERIT`, and always as `Base:MemberName`; it cannot stand alone.
rules.rationale:
`Base` names the parent class's members. A class with no `:INHERIT` has no
parent, and `Base` on its own is not a value.

rules.title: Underscore prefix marks private members
rules.rule: Underscore-prefixed members (`_name`) are excluded from reflection — this is the SSL private convention.
rules.rationale:
Class methods are always public, and access modifiers have no effect on them.
The `_` prefix is the only way to keep a member out of reflection-based
access.

rules.title: Do not name a class after a built-in class
rules.rule: Do not give a `:CLASS` the name of a built-in class such as `Email` or `SSLDataset`.
rules.rationale:
A class named like a built-in confuses readers, who reach for `Email{}` and
get the wrong one.

rules.title: Class fields are declared at class level
rules.rule: Declare class fields with `:DECLARE` at class level, not inside methods.
rules.rationale:
Only a `:DECLARE` at class level creates a field. The same statement inside a
method declares a local variable that disappears when the method returns, so
`Me:` never sees it.

rules.title: Fields and properties are different things
rules.rule: Use field for `:DECLARE` slots on classes, and reserve property for dynamic-object members, `SSLExpando` members, and `AddProperty`-created members.
rules.rationale:
Class fields and dynamic-object properties are separate runtime mechanisms.
Calling both "properties" in a review or a spec hides which one the code
uses.

good.code:
Counter keeps its total in the field nCount (Me:nCount).
The request object carries the property orderNo, added with AddProperty.

bad.code: Counter keeps its total in the property nCount.

rules.title: Built-in classes instantiate with curly braces
rules.rule: Instantiate directly creatable built-in classes with curly braces, for example `Email{}`.
rules.rationale:
Built-in classes are constructed with `ClassName{args}`. Parentheses make a
function call, and there is no function by that name.
rules.exceptions:
`SSLExpando` and `SSLBaseDictionary` have no direct constructor; see the
schema's `no_direct_constructor`.

good.code:
:DECLARE oEmail;

oEmail := Email{};

bad.code:
:DECLARE oEmail;
oEmail := Email();

rules.title: Built-in functions keep their documented casing
rules.rule: Represent functions in PascalCase where applicable, while preserving canonical exceptions such as `_AND`, `_OR`, `_XOR`, `_NOT`, `DOW`, `DOY`, and `LIMSDate`.
rules.rationale:
Function names are case-insensitive, so any casing runs. The documented
casing makes code searchable and consistent with the reference.

good.code:
:DECLARE sName;

sName := AllTrim(" a ");

bad.code:
:DECLARE sName;
sName := ALLTRIM(" a ");

rules.title: Procedures and classes are PascalCase
rules.rule: Procedures and classes use PascalCase.
rules.rationale:
PascalCase separates procedure and class names from prefixed variables at a
glance.

rules.title: Hungarian camelCase variable names
rules.rule: Variables use Hungarian-style camelCase: a type prefix, then a camelCase body (`sMyVar`, not `s_my_var` or `SMYVAR`).
rules.rationale:
The prefix tells the reader the type without a lookup, and the camelCase body
keeps names readable in a case-insensitive language.
rules.exceptions:
Declared loop counters (see `loop_counter_names`), constants, and the literals
`NIL`, `.T.` and `.F.`.

rules.title: Constants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
rules.rule: Constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE.
rules.rationale:
Uppercase names mark a value that is set once and read many times, and they
take no type prefix.

good.code:
:DECLARE MAX_ATTEMPTS;

MAX_ATTEMPTS := 3;

bad.code:
:DECLARE maxAttempts;
maxAttempts := 3;

rules.title: Use the documented type prefixes
rules.rule: Use documented prefixes: `s`, `n`, `b`, `d`, `a`, `o`, `fn`, and `v`.
rules.rationale:
A shared, small set of prefixes is what makes a prefix meaningful to every
reader and to the type checks that read it.

rules.title: No renames in a behavior-preserving refactor
rules.rule: Do not rename values in behavior-preserving refactors unless the refactor scope includes naming cleanup.
rules.rationale:
A rename touches every use of a name, which buries the real change in a large
diff and can break callers that reach the name dynamically.

good.code:
Refactor scope: extract the validation into a procedure. Variable names are
left as they were.

bad.code:
Refactor scope: extract the validation into a procedure. The diff also
renames cnt to nCount across the file.

rules.title: A prefix matches the value's type
rules.rule: Make a variable's prefix match the type of the value it holds: `s` string, `n` numeric, `b` boolean, `d` date, `a` array, `o` object, `fn` code block, `v` variant/any.
rules.rationale:
A prefix that disagrees with the value misleads every reader, and usually
points to a real type error.

good.code:
:DECLARE nCount;

nCount := 0;

bad.code:
:DECLARE sCount;
sCount := 0;

rules.title: Identifier length limits
rules.rule: Keep variable names to 20 characters after the type prefix, and procedure and function names to 30 characters.
rules.rationale:
Short names fit on a line next to the code that uses them. The limit counts
the body after the prefix, so the prefix never costs a character.

good.code:
:DECLARE sCustomerOrderNo;

sCustomerOrderNo := "A1";

bad.code:
:DECLARE sCustomerOrderNumberXY;
sCustomerOrderNumberXY := "A1";

rules.title: Single-letter loop counters
rules.rule: Loop counters may be `i`, `j`, `k`, `x`, `y` or `z` without a prefix only when declared; in a script that calls other scripts, prefer a script-specific name such as `nSampleIdx`.
rules.rationale:
An undeclared counter is looked up in the callers' scopes, so it can collide
with a caller's variable of the same name.

rules.title: Preserve established acronym casing
rules.rule: Preserve established acronym casing only when it already exists in the surrounding codebase or required external names.
rules.rationale:
Matching an acronym's existing casing keeps a name consistent with the code
and external names around it; new names follow the normal camelCase body.

bad.code: New code in a script that writes sQcStatus everywhere introduces sQCStatus.

rules.title: User-defined object properties are lowerCamelCase
rules.rule: Name user-defined object properties in lowerCamelCase with no type prefix, for example `oOrder:orderNo`.
rules.rationale:
Property names read as part of the object expression, and the object variable
already carries the type prefix.

rules.title: Avoid underscores in variable and procedure names
rules.rule: Avoid underscores in variable and procedure names; file-level suffixes such as `_Core` and `_Batch` are standard.
rules.rationale:
The naming convention separates words with case, not underscores. Constants
and the `_` private-member prefix are the exceptions.

rules.title: Procedure names are verb plus noun
rules.rule: Name procedures as a verb followed by a noun, for example `ValidateOrder`, `ProcessQCSample` or `CalculateTotal`.
rules.rationale:
A verb and a noun say what the procedure does and to what, so a call reads as
an action.
